sens: The act of breaking bread into pieces
The ritual gesture of sharing bread during a meal
The central act of the Christian communion meal
G2800.detail:
1. Literally, it is the physical action of breaking bread into pieces with one's hands. At the moment when the resurrected Jesus breaks the bread before the disciples of Emmaus, they recognize him by this gesture (Luke 24:35): it is a simple and everyday act that suddenly takes on particular significance.
2. This gesture is not trivial: in Jewish culture, the one who breaks the bread presides over the meal and sanctifies it. It is an act of responsibility and authority.
3. For the early Christians, this "breaking of bread" becomes the key expression of their communion (Acts 2:42). It designates both the shared meal and the memorial of Jesus' death and resurrection. It is no longer just a technical gesture, but a spiritual act that unites the assembly.
G2800.origine: The word comes from the verb κλάω (klao: to break, to shatter). The breaking of bread is the visible gesture of what is broken — the bread into pieces, but also, in the Christian sense, the body given of Christ. It is a rich biblical image: the whole bread becomes several parts to nourish many people, an image of sharing and sacrifice.
G2800.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, at two key moments in the life of the early Church. In Luke 24:35, it is the concrete gesture by which Jesus reveals himself to the disciples. In Acts 2:42, it is one of the four fundamental activities of the nascent Church: they devote themselves to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer. This term thus becomes a name to designate the Eucharistic practice of the Church.
G2800.portee: This simple gesture of broken bread reminds us that the Christian faith is expressed in tangible and shared acts. For the first disciples, recognizing Jesus at this precise moment shows that the risen Christ is present in the humble gestures of sharing. For us, the breaking of bread invites us to see in each Eucharistic communion the living presence of Christ and the unity of his body, which is the Church.

sens: fragment of bread or food after breaking
leftover food after a meal
debris, waste
G2801.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a fragment of bread or food that has been broken, shattered. It is the physical result of the action of breaking or dividing: when Jesus multiplies the loaves, the disciples collect the leftover pieces (Matthew 14:20).
2. By extension, it refers to the leftover food after a meal, what remains on the plate or table. The Gospels use this word to describe the leftovers from the two miracles of multiplication (five thousand men and four thousand men), piled in full baskets — a remarkable abundance (Mark 8:19-20).
3. The meaning broadens to include any debris or food waste: what has not been consumed and needs to be collected. The emphasis on these twelve and seven baskets of pieces highlights how Jesus' blessing produced an abundance, not scarcity.
G2801.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "klàô" which means "to break, to shatter, to rupture." It literally means "what has been broken." The suffix "-ma" forms neuter nouns from verbs: it designates the result of the action. The word translates the Hebrew "patt" (piece of bread) and "pélach" (fragment, slice).
G2801.emploi: This word appears only nine times in the New Testament, exclusively in the four Gospels. It mainly recurs in the two accounts of the multiplication of the loaves (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John), always to describe the collected leftovers. The usage is very concrete and practical: no symbolism, just a material observation. Mark repeats this word to emphasize Jesus' question to the disciples: "How many baskets full of pieces did you take up?" (Mark 8:19-20). John adds a touching detail: the disciples gather the pieces "so that nothing is lost" (John 6:12).
G2801.portee: These collected pieces are not an insignificant detail. Their abundance and the care taken to gather them reveal the generosity of Christ: He does not multiply the loaves sparingly, but lavishly. For the Christian reader, it is a lesson in trust: Christ never produces just the right portion, but abundance. And the act of gathering everything up ("so that nothing is lost") speaks of a divine economy where nothing that God gives is wasted or thrown away.

sens: Small island near Crete
G2802.detail: Clauda is a small island located near Crete in the Mediterranean. It appears only once in the Bible, during the tumultuous journey of the apostle Paul to Rome as a prisoner. The ship carrying him passes near this island, and the passage mentions that the sailors had difficulty managing the lifeboat due to the violent wind blowing around Clauda (Acts 27:16).
G2802.origine: Clauda is the Greek name of a small Mediterranean island. It is a geographical name of ancient origin, known to sailors and geographers of antiquity. The island was a notable landmark for ships navigating the maritime routes near Crete.
G2802.emploi: Clauda appears only once in the entire New Testament, in Acts 27:16. It is mentioned in the account of Paul's perilous journey to Rome in chapter 27 of Acts, where the ship runs aground during a storm. The mention of Clauda is brief but geographically precise: the ship passes beneath (or near) this small island, and it is at this moment that the crew faces difficulties securing the ship's lifeboat. This geographical detail contributes to the historical authenticity of the travel narrative.

sens: Christian woman of the early church mentioned in the last verses of Paul's second epistle to Timothy
G2803.detail: Claudia is a believer from Rome who sends her greetings to Timothy through Paul. She is listed among a small group of faithful who remained by the apostle's side: Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, and herself. This brief mention suggests that despite Paul's increasing isolation at the end of his life, a few brothers and sisters remain faithful to him and are committed to supporting him.
G2803.origine: Claudia is a Latin name borne by several people in Roman times. In France and the Francophone Christian world, this name simply refers to this woman known only through this short passage of the epistle.
G2803.emploi: Claudia appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:21. Paul, at the end of his life and in prison, lists the few faithful companions who remain with him. Claudia is explicitly named, which means that her faith and support for the apostle were remarkable and worthy of mention. It is a testimony of encouragement for Timothy in his own ministry.
G2803.portee: The mention of Claudia reminds us that faithfulness to Christ is not visible or spectacular, but deep and constant. It also shows that in the early church, women played an active and recognized role in community life and in supporting the apostles.

sens: The Roman emperor who reigned from 41 to 54 AD
The Roman military tribune in charge of Jerusalem
G2804G.detail:
1. Claudius is the Roman emperor during the apostolic era: it is under his reign that a great famine strikes the earth (Acts 11:28), and he is the one who ordered the expulsion of all Jews from Rome, which led Aquila and Priscilla to leave Italy (Acts 18:2). His reign is historically situated between 41 and 54 AD.
2. Claudius Lysias is a military tribune, that is, a Roman officer commanding a garrison: he is mentioned as the military chief present at the arrest of Paul in Jerusalem (Acts 23:26).
G2804G.origine: Claudius comes from the Latin Claudius, a Roman cognomen (nickname) borne by several emperors and notable Romans. The name derives from the Latin claudus, which means "lame," but in Roman culture, it was simply a family name without this pejorative connotation. The French Segond uses the spelling "Claude" to refer to these two Roman figures in the New Testament.
G2804G.emploi: The name Claudius appears twice in the New Testament. The first mention (Acts 11:28) refers to Emperor Claudius who rules over Rome at the time of the famine reported by the prophet Agabus. The second (Acts 18:2) refers to the same emperor and his decree expelling the Jews from Rome. A third usage mentions Claudius Lysias (Acts 23:26), a distinct Roman military tribune from the emperor, who commanded the garrison in Jerusalem. These two figures represent Roman authority in the context of the early Church's beginnings.
G2804G.portee: The mention of Claudius highlights how the story of the young apostolic Church fits within the political framework of the Roman Empire. The emperor's decrees directly affect the lives of Christians and Jews: a famine strikes the entire known world, and an expulsion scatters communities. These references anchor the biblical narrative in verifiable history and show that believers live under earthly powers that, unknowingly, serve God's purposes.

sens: Roman emperor of the 1st century
Roman military tribune
G2804H.detail:
1. Claudius is the name of a Roman emperor who reigned in the 1st century AD. Luke mentions him in Acts 11:28 during a famine that struck the entire world under his reign — a well-documented historical event.
2. Claudius is also the nickname or honorific title of the military tribune C. Lysias, mentioned in Acts 23:26 when he writes to Governor Felix about Paul. It is a mark of respect to use it in official correspondence.
G2804H.origine: Claudius is a Latin name borne by several important figures in Roman history. In biblical Hebrew, there is no equivalent: it is a pure borrowing from Latin, natural in a Roman context. The name evokes the idea of lameness or claudication, but this etymology is uncertain; more likely, it comes from a well-established ancient Roman family.
G2804H.emploi: The name "Claude" or "Claudius" appears twice in the New Testament, always in relation to Roman rule. First as the title of the emperor under whose reign a great famine struck the inhabited earth (Acts 11:28), which helps us date the event. Then, it is the honorific title of tribune Lysias when he officially corresponds with Governor Felix regarding the apostle Paul in detention at Caesarea (Acts 23:26). In this latter case, it is a title of politeness or military rank, not a confusion of identities.

sens: The act of crying, the tears that flow from the face
The visible expression of sadness, grief
The manifestation of pain during a separation or loss
In the language of Jesus, the eternal suffering and despair of the reprobate
G2805.detail:
1. The act of crying is primarily the physical phenomenon of tears: to cry is to shed tears from the face in reaction to a strong emotion. When Paul leaves the elders of Ephesus, "there were abundant tears" (Acts 20:37): it is the concrete spectacle of tears shed out of affection.
2. The act of crying especially expresses a deep suffering of the heart. When Matthew reports Jeremiah, "Rachel weeps for her children" (Matthew 2:18): these are not just tears, but the manifestation of a mother’s mourning and grief for her sons.
3. The Bible often uses "weeping and gnashing of teeth" together to describe absolute distress. This expression appears in several of Jesus' parables (Matthew 8:12, 13:42, 22:13, 24:51, 25:30, Luke 13:28): it paints the situation of the reprobate at judgment, combining extreme moral suffering with helplessness and rage.
G2805.origine: The word comes from the verb "to cry" (κλαίω) and designates the resultant action: weeping is what arises from the act of crying. In Hebrew, the same word (בְּכִי) is used for tears and lamentation. This family of words belongs to the register of direct human emotions, without abstraction: weeping is a reality of the body and heart, visible and concrete.
G2805.emploi: The word "weeping" appears 9 times in the Greek New Testament, mostly in Matthew (6 times). Three usages stand out: first, the tears of mourning (Matthew 2:18, Acts 20:37); then, tears of intense affliction; and finally and especially, in the phrase "weeping and gnashing of teeth," the image of the misfortune of the reprobate on the day of judgment. This last usage, typical of Jesus' teaching, recurs to signify separation from God and irretrievable loss.
G2805.portee: For the Christian, tears remind us that sadness and mourning are recognized and legitimate in human experience — even Paul sheds tears before his brothers. But the image of "weeping" at judgment also warns of the seriousness of divine justice: rejecting Jesus leads to a permanent suffering from which no comforter can deliver us. This perspective gives urgency to repentance and gratitude for God's mercy.

sens: To break something into pieces
To share bread by breaking it
To celebrate together by breaking bread
G2806.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to break, to fragment something solid by dividing it with force. It is the physical action of breaking: when Jesus "breaks" the loaves at the multiplication, he "breaks" them to make portions (Matthew 14:19).
2. Quickly, the word specialized to designate the act of breaking bread at the table, that is, sharing it among the guests before a meal. This very common gesture, fundamental in Jewish and Mediterranean culture, becomes an act of communion and sharing.
3. In the life of the early Church, "breaking bread" becomes an expression that designates the Lord's Supper, the Eucharist, or the breaking of bread: the disciples "broke bread in their homes" every day (Acts 2:46), celebrating their faith together.
G2806.origine: The verb κλάω comes from a root that expresses the action of breaking, fragmenting. In Hebrew, the corresponding verb (פרר, especially in its derivatives) also carries this idea of rupture. The word is simple and direct: it describes a common physical gesture, that of breaking, which gradually becomes a rich symbol in Christian worship.
G2806.emploi: The verb appears 14 times in the New Testament, exclusively to speak of broken bread. In the four Gospels, Jesus "breaks" the bread during the multiplications of loaves and at the Last Supper (Matthew 14:19, 26:26; Mark 8:6, 14:22; Luke 22:19; Luke 24:30). In Acts, the disciples imitate this gesture by gathering: "breaking bread" becomes the central act of their communal life and their memorial of the risen Christ (Acts 2:46, 20:7, 20:11, 27:35). Paul, in 1 Corinthians, explicates the significance: the broken bread is the body of Christ shared (1 Corinthians 10:16, 11:24). The physical and everyday gesture is transfigured into an act of faith.
G2806.portee: This word invites the believer to see in the simple gesture of breaking bread the depth of Christ's sacrifice. The breaking of bread is not an empty ritual, but the living memory of Jesus' gift: his body given, broken, shared for the life of the world. This connects heaven and the table, transforming a culinary act into an act of worship and fraternal communion.

sens: Metal object that opens and closes a lock
Authority that allows access to a place or power
Access to knowledge or understanding
Control or mastery over something
G2807.detail:
1. In the literal sense, a key is the metal object that opens a door or closes a lock: it is the concrete instrument of passage and access control.

2. In a figurative sense, having the keys means holding authority and power over a domain. Jesus says to Peter: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 16:19), which means entrusting him with the authority to welcome or exclude from the kingdom of God.

3. The key also represents access to understanding and wisdom. Jesus reproaches the teachers of the law for having "taken away the key of knowledge" (Luke 11:52): they block access to the true knowledge of God.

4. Finally, the key signifies control or dominion over a power or domain. The Resurrected One holds "the keys of death and Hades" (Revelation 1:18), meaning he has absolute power over death. Similarly, the angel who descends holds "the key to the abyss" (Revelation 20:1) to seal the rebellion of Satan.
G2807.origine: The word κλείς comes from an ancient Greek root meaning the action of closing and locking. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the word מַפְתֵּחַ (maftéah, "key") is found, which has the same imagery: the object that closes and opens. The key is the instrument of access power, hence its metaphorical use to denote any form of authority or control in the Bible.
G2807.emploi: The word κλείς (key) appears 6 times in the New Testament, always in a figurative context: never for a simple door key. Jesus speaks of it to Peter to symbolize spiritual authority (Matthew 16:19). The risen Lord possesses it over death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). The word also describes Christ's power over the house of David (Revelation 3:7): it is an image of his messianic royal authority. Finally, apocalyptic visions mention the keys of the abyss or the bottomless pit (Revelation 9:1; 20:1) to show who dominates the powers of evil and chaos. In all these cases, the key symbolizes a power of control and access.
G2807.portee: Understanding the word "key" helps the Christian grasp what Jesus confers to spiritual leaders and the Church: not arbitrary power, but a sacred responsibility to open access to the kingdom of God. It also reminds us that only the Resurrected One holds the true keys over death and sin: our ultimate security rests in him, not in human institutions. The refusal of the key of knowledge (Luke 11:52) warns that blocking the Gospel is a serious sin.

sens: Close a door, an entrance, a building
Close the heavens, stop the rain
Close the bowels, withhold help
Close the kingdom, refuse access to salvation
G2808.detail:
1. The primary sense is physical: to close a door or an entrance. Jesus commands to close the door when praying (Matthew 6:6), the temple doors close during the riot against Paul (Acts 21:30), and after the resurrection, Jesus passes through the closed doors of the disciples' house (John 20:26).

2. Figuratively, closing the heavens means stopping the rain. Elijah, by the power of God, closes the heavens for three and a half years, causing a great famine (Luke 4:25). It is an image of divine dominion over nature.

3. Closing the bowels or compassion means withholding help and love from those in need. John writes that anyone who has the goods of this world and closes his compassion against his brother does not have the love of God in him (1 John 3:17). It is to refuse to give, to assist.

4. In a spiritual sense, closing the kingdom means refusing entry to salvation. Jesus reproaches the religious leaders for closing the kingdom of heaven to men (Matthew 23:13). Only Christ, who has the key of David, truly opens and closes access to the kingdom (Revelation 3:7).
G2808.origine: The verb κλείω comes from a root that expresses the action of closing, locking. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates סָגַר (sagar), which denotes both the physical closing of a door and the locking of the heavens or the heart. The family of the word includes κλείς (the key) and κλῆσις (the call, in the sense of what calls to enter or to stay outside). The basic image is that of closure which separates, isolates, refuses, or forbids access.
G2808.emploi: The verb κλείω appears about fifteen times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. In the literal sense, it describes the closing of doors (house, temple, prison) and that of the underground boat (Revelation 20:3). In the figurative sense, it expresses divine action or that of religious leaders: closing the heavens (Luke 4:25), closing access to the kingdom (Matthew 23:13-14, Revelation 3:7-8), or withholding help from the suffering (1 John 3:17). Revelation 21:25 affirms that in the new city, the gates will never be closed, an image of permanent access to salvation.
G2808.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on two doors. First, closing the door of one's room to pray in secret: it is intimacy with God, away from human eyes. Secondly, not closing one's heart to those who suffer, but keeping compassion open. It also reminds us that only Christ, who holds the key of David, truly decides who enters or remains outside the kingdom of God.

sens: Action of stealing what belongs to another
Stolen thing
G2809.detail:
1. Theft is the act of taking what belongs to someone else, secretly or fraudulently. It is an act of theft in the common sense of the term, one of the actions condemned by God's law. In Revelation 9:21, people refuse to repent of their thefts among other serious sins: murders, sorceries, fornication.
2. The word can also refer to the stolen thing itself, the object that has been taken. This meaning is less common in the New Testament, but it emphasizes that everything taken unjustly belongs to the one who is stolen from.
G2809.origine: The Greek word κλέμμα comes from the verb κλέπτω, "to steal" (from which also derives the noun κλέψ, a thief, hence the French "kleptomaniac"). In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often renders the same concept by גָּנַב (ganab), used for example in Genesis 31:39 for stolen livestock. The root expresses the idea of taking furtively, in secret.
G2809.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 9:21, in the plural ("thefts"). John lists there the serious sins of which people refuse to repent: murders, sorceries, debauchery, and thefts. This context shows that theft is not a minor sin, but one of the transgressions that distances man from God and for which repentance is necessary. The absence of this word elsewhere in the New Testament contrasts with the frequency of the verb κλέπτω ("to steal") and the noun κλέψ ("thief").
G2809.portee: For the believer, the mention of theft among the major sins from which one must repent reminds us that the property of others is sacred in the eyes of God. It is a call to honesty and justice in our economic and material relationships, not only in manifest acts but also in the small dishonesties of daily life.

sens: Disciple who encountered the resurrected Jesus on the road to Emmaus
G2810.detail: Cleopas is one of the two disciples who were walking to the village of Emmaus on the day of Jesus' resurrection. With his companion (whose name is not given), he was discussing the events of the crucifixion when Jesus himself joined them without them recognizing him. It is Cleopas who speaks up to express his astonishment that a visitor is unaware of "what has happened there these days" — the extraordinary events in Jerusalem (Luke 24:18).
G2810.origine: The name Κλεόπας (Kleopas) is an abbreviated form of the Greek name Κλεόπατρος. It literally means "glory of the father" (from κλέος, "glory," and πάτρος, "father"). It is a common name in the Greco-Roman world.
G2810.emploi: Cleopas appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 24:18. He is one of the two disciples heading to Emmaus after the crucifixion of Jesus. Ancient Christian tradition, though not confirmed by Scripture, has often identified his companion with other disciples, but the Bible does not name him. This man is a crucial witness to the resurrection, as Jesus explains to him how all the Scriptures concerned him, and later he recognizes him in the breaking of the bread.
G2810.portee: Cleopas' encounter with the resurrected Jesus reminds us that the resurrection was not initially evident to the disciples themselves: their faith had to be built up through the progressive revelation of Christ. This story also highlights the importance of the Christian community — even "ordinary" disciples, not just the apostles, received direct teaching from the risen Lord and became witnesses to what transformed the world.

sens: What is spoken of, the reputation one leaves behind
Esteem and honor earned through one's actions
Renown, good reputation gained and carried
G2811.detail:
1. This word primarily refers to what is talked about, what is said regarding someone: it is the rumor, the reputation one leaves behind. It is the image of the word that circulates about you.
2. This word becomes glory when it is good, that is, when it honors you. In 1 Peter 2:20, Paul speaks of enduring suffering for having done well: "this is a grace in the sight of God." This kind of glory is the honor that God sees in you and that deserves to be recognized.
3. More broadly, it is the good reputation acquired through worthy actions and carried as a precious possession. It is what one leaves behind that is worthy of esteem.
G2811.origine: The Greek word kleos comes from an ancient root that expresses the idea of what is said, of what is heard. It literally designates what is proclaimed or what is proclaimed about someone. In the Septuagint, it translates the Hebrew שֵׁמַע (shema, to hear, noise), which shows that glory is what is heard being said, what is talked about.
G2811.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 2:20. Peter uses it to describe the honor that comes from enduring unjust suffering while doing good: it is not a glory to be punished for doing wrong, but it is a glory to be punished for obeying God. It is the glory that God recognizes and welcomes. This meaning aligns with that of the renown acquired through one's actions: a righteous life leaves a beautiful reputation.
G2811.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that true glory is not the worldly reputation one seeks to acquire, but the good renown earned by doing what is right, even if it costs. It is a call to live in such a way as to leave a lasting glory before God and before men.

sens: One who stealthily takes the property of others
Who acts in secret, by cunning or fraud
One who comes unexpectedly, without warning
Figuratively: false teacher, spiritual seducer
Symbol of suddenness and the unexpected
G2812.detail:
1. A thief is someone who takes the property of others secretly, without open violence: this contrasts with a robber who plunders by force. Jesus warns his disciples that thieves can break into a house (Matthew 24:43), hence the importance of being vigilant and not storing up treasures on earth (Matthew 6:19).
2. The word emphasizes the hidden and fraudulent nature of theft: John reports that Judas, who held the disciples' purse, "was a thief" (John 12:6), secretly drawing from the common funds.
3. The image of the thief coming unexpectedly becomes a powerful biblical comparison: the day of the Lord will come "like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2), suddenly, without prior announcement, hence the necessity of vigilance.
4. Jesus uses "thief" figuratively to refer to false prophets or spiritual guides who seduce the sheep by cunning (John 10:8), distinct from the true shepherd who enters through the door.
5. The notion of suddenness implicit in the thief illustrates the idea that divine intervention in history occurs at an unexpected hour, requiring constant vigilance.
G2812.origine: The word κλέπτης (kleptēs) comes from the root κλέπ- which means "to steal, to rob" and designates one who acts by theft and cunning, in secret. It translates the Hebrew גַּנָּב (gannāb). Unlike a robber (λῃστής, lēstēs) who steals openly and by violence, the thief steals by fraud and cunning, which explains why the word applies both to unfaithful Judas and to the unexpected coming of the Lord.
G2812.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Luke, and John. It primarily designates ordinary criminals: those who break into houses (Matthew 6:19-20, Matthew 24:43, Luke 12:39) and whom the apostle Paul classifies among those who will not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:10, 1 Peter 4:15). However, the Bible mostly uses it figuratively and spiritually: Judas the thief (John 12:6), false prophets who are thieves (John 10:8), and especially the day of the Lord coming "like a thief" (1 Thessalonians 5:2, 2 Peter 3:10, Revelation 3:3, Revelation 16:15). In these apocalyptic passages, the word carries no moral judgment: it simply expresses the unexpected and the suddenness.
G2812.portee: Understanding that Jesus speaks of true thieves — those who steal material goods — teaches us not to cling to them (Matthew 6:19), for eternal treasure cannot be stolen. But above all, the term "thief" applied to the day of the Lord invites every believer to a constant spiritual vigilance: the hour cannot be predicted, one must live in a state of readiness, far from the riches of the world. Finally, the warning against "thieves" (false teachers) teaches us to discern who truly enters through the door of Christ.

sens: To take someone else's property secretly, to steal
To fraudulently appropriate something that belongs to another
In a spiritual sense, to deprive someone of what is due to them
G2813.detail:
1. To steal means to take secretly what belongs to someone else. It is the act of a thief who acts without permission and without paying. Jesus warns against thieves who break into houses to steal earthly treasures (Matthew 6:19).
2. The word is also used for the fraudulent appropriation of a specific good: for example, the disciples could have stolen the body of Jesus from the tomb (Matthew 27:64).
3. In a moral and spiritual sense, to steal means to deprive someone of their due, to take away what rightfully belongs to them. This is why Paul instructs those who steal to stop doing so and to instead work to earn their bread so they can give to those in need (Ephesians 4:28).
G2813.origine: The Greek verb kleptō comes from a root that evokes the action of taking secretly. In ancient Hebrew, the corresponding word is ganab, which appears in the commandments prohibiting theft. The Greek verb retains this fundamental meaning: to take what does not belong to you, to act secretly against the will of the owner.
G2813.emploi: The verb kleptō appears eleven times in the New Testament, always to denote the act of stealing or taking away. It is first found in the words of Jesus: he uses it when he speaks of thieves who break into houses (Matthew 6:19-20) or that the disciples could have come to steal his body (Matthew 27:64 and 28:13). The verb also appears in the reminder of the commandments of the Decalogue, notably "You shall not steal" (Matthew 19:18, Mark 10:19). Paul uses it to urge thieves to stop stealing and to work honestly (Ephesians 4:28) and to recall the law against theft (Romans 13:9). John uses it when he quotes Jesus saying that the thief comes only to steal (John 10:10). In every occurrence, the meaning remains the same: to take someone else's property without right or permission.
G2813.portee: This word reminds Christians of the importance of honesty and respect for the property of others, a commandment rooted in God's law since Sinai. For those who have turned away from theft due to sin, the Gospel offers conversion: to stop stealing and work to meet their needs and help others. It is an invitation to justice and generosity rather than greed.

sens: Vine branch that bears grapes
Living part of the plant that depends on its root and trunk
Symbol of one who belongs to Christ and produces spiritual fruit
G2814.detail:
1. The branch is literally the vine branch, the one that develops from the vine or trunk, and directly bears the grapes. In John 15:2, Jesus speaks of "every branch that is in me" to refer to the branches attached to the vine, some of which bear fruit and others do not.
2. The branch exists only through its connection to the vine: it can live and bear fruit only if it remains attached to the mother plant (John 15:4). This dependence is absolute and natural — the branch alone, separated from the vine, can do nothing and withers (John 15:6).
3. Jesus uses the image of the branch to speak of believers: "you are the branches" (John 15:5). The disciples are the living branches of the vine that is Christ; their spiritual fruitfulness depends entirely on their union with him, and those who do not remain in him are thrown away and burned (John 15:6).
G2814.origine: The Greek word klēma comes from a root meaning "to break" or "to bend": the branch is what bends and branches out. In Hebrew, words like zemōrāh or dāliyyāh also refer to vine branches. The Greek word emphasizes the living and flexible nature of the branch, capable of growing and bearing fruit.
G2814.emploi: The word appears four times, all in the discourse of the vine and branches in John 15 (verses 2, 4, 5, 6). Jesus constructs a complete parable: the branches are in him, they must remain attached to him to bear fruit, and those who detach or do not bear fruit are cut off and burned in the fire. It is an image to teach the disciples the necessity of union with him and spiritual dependence. The term remains very concrete — it is really about vine branches — while carrying a clear spiritual meaning.
G2814.portee: This image of the branch reminds Christians that they can accomplish nothing lasting and spiritually fruitful if they do not remain in Christ. It invites us to examine our attachment to him and the quality of our dependence: are we truly connected to the root of our life? It also teaches that the pruning of unproductive branches is an act of love from the Father, intended for greater fruitfulness (John 15:2).

sens: Co-worker of the apostle Paul in Philippi
G2815.detail: Clement is a Christian from the church in Philippi who worked alongside Paul for the Gospel. Paul mentions him in Philippians 4:3 as one of those who "struggled for the Gospel" with him, alongside two pious women (Euodia and Syntyche) whose disagreements he asks the recipient of the letter to reconcile. He is a faithful servant of whom Paul says that his name is "written in the book of life" — an expression of his assurance that Clement belongs to the people of God and will participate in eternal salvation.
G2815.origine: The name Clement comes from the Latin "clemens," which means "merciful, gentle." It is a common Roman name given to this Christian from Philippi, a city in Macedonia where Jews and Greeks converted to faith in Jesus met.
G2815.emploi: Clement appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 4:3. Paul designates him as a trusted collaborator in the service of the Gospel in Philippi. The context shows that he was respected and recognized for his commitment alongside Paul and the local church. Some early patristic traditions have wanted to see him as one of the first bishops or pastors of the church in Philippi, but the Bible provides no other biographical details.
G2815.portee: Clement illustrates the discreet yet valuable role of faithful collaborators in the expansion of the Gospel. Although he is mentioned only once, Paul bestows lasting dignity upon him by linking his name to the "book of life" — a reminder that every servant engaged in God's work, whether known or forgotten by men, is counted and loved by the Lord.

sens: To receive something as an inheritance, by right of succession.
To possess, obtain something as one's own.
To enter into possession of the kingdom of God and its eternal blessings.
G2816.detail:
1. In its primary sense, to inherit means to receive property or land by family succession, as one would after the death of a relative (Galatians 4:30). It is to receive what was intended for a family or lineage.

2. More broadly, the word means to obtain or possess something as one's own (Matthew 25:34: "inherit the kingdom"). It expresses the idea of making one's own what was promised or reserved.

3. In the New Testament, to inherit primarily refers to entering into eternal life and God's promises: the land (Matthew 5:5), eternal life (Luke 10:25), the kingdom of God (Matthew 25:34, 1 Corinthians 6:9). It is to receive the promised blessings of salvation in Christ. Believers are called to inherit these riches, while those who live in sin will not inherit them (1 Corinthians 15:50: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom).
G2816.origine: The Greek word κληρονομέω comes from κληρονόμος (one who receives an inheritance), formed from κλῆρος (the lot, the portion that belongs) and νέμω (to distribute). The original image is that of drawing lots or distributing a share. In Hebrew, this verb primarily translates יָרַשׁ (yarash: to take possession) and נָחַל (nakhal: to receive as an inheritance). These Hebrew roots trace back to the idea of occupying the promised land.
G2816.emploi: The verb κληρονομέω appears 17 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Paul, and the epistles. It is rarely used in the purely legal sense of material inheritance; it is almost always spiritualized. Believers are called to inherit the kingdom of God (Matthew 25:34, Galatians 5:21), eternal life (Luke 10:25, Matthew 19:29), and divine blessing (Hebrews 12:17, 1 Peter 3:9). Paul emphasizes that certain groups (the unjust, those of flesh and blood) will not inherit the kingdom (1 Corinthians 6:9, 15:50). In the author of Hebrews, the word underscores the promise to believers: they will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14) and God's promises (Hebrews 6:12).
G2816.portee: This word reminds the believer that eternal life and the kingdom of God are not a personal acquisition, but a promise inherited in Christ. It is a call to moral vigilance: only those who renounce sin and trust in God can inherit it. The verb transforms the relationship with God: the believer does not earn their salvation; they receive it as a gift, as an inheritance prepared by the Father. It is both a privilege and a spiritual responsibility.

sens: property passed from a deceased person to their heirs
possession, real property
the blessings of the Kingdom of God granted to believers
G2817.detail:
1. In a concrete sense, inheritance is a property — land, wealth — that someone receives after the death of the person who owned it. In the parable of the tenants, they say upon seeing the owner's son: "Here comes the heir; come, let us kill him and seize his inheritance" (Matthew 21:38) — they want to appropriate the land he would have received.
2. The word extends to any possession or real property, not just what is passed down by succession. When Abraham asks for possession of the land, God "gave him no inheritance in it, not even enough to set his foot on" (Acts 7:5), but promises to give it to his descendants — it concerns the promised lands.
3. In the Christian faith, inheritance becomes the image of the eternal blessings that God promises to believers. Paul speaks of "the inheritance" we will receive from the Lord as a reward (Colossians 3:24), and of "the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints" (Ephesians 1:18) — this is eternal life and the goods of the Kingdom. This figurative sense shows that God treats believers as his children, who will inherit all that he possesses.
G2817.origine: The Greek word comes from klêros ("lot", "portion") and nomos ("law", "usage"), literally meaning "what is assigned by lot" — in ancient law, a father's inheritance was divided among the sons according to established rules, like a drawn lot. It translates the Hebrew nahalah ("hereditary possession"), which in the Old Testament primarily refers to the land promised to Israel and passed down through generations.
G2817.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament. In the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke), it retains its legal sense: the inheritance of an owner (Matthew 21:38, Luke 12:13). Paul uses it primarily in a spiritual sense to describe God's gift to believers (Galatians 3:18: the inheritance promised to Abraham comes from the promise, not from the law; Colossians 3:24: eternal reward for service). In Ephesians and Hebrews, it refers to the riches of salvation reserved by God for the saints (Ephesians 1:14, 1:18; Hebrews 9:15). The word thus enriches itself: from the concrete (earthly goods) to the spiritual (blessings of God).
G2817.portee: This word reveals that salvation in Christ is not a one-time favor, but an entry into a family — that of God. Believers are made heirs, which means lasting security and dignity: they receive not by purchase or effort, but as children. It is also an incentive: to serve the Lord generously, for true wealth is what God reserves for the saints in eternity.

sens: one who receives an inheritance, a property left by the one who possessed it
one who possesses or has a right to something by succession or promise
in a spiritual sense, one who receives the blessings and promises of God
Christ, who inherits all things from his Father
G2818.detail:
1. An heir is primarily one who legally receives a property — land, wealth, status — after the death of the one who possessed it. In the parable of the tenants (Matthew 21:38), the servants kill the son because he is the heir of his father's vineyard.
2. By extension, it is one who possesses something by right or by succession, even before the death of the one from whom he depends. A minor child remains under guardianship even though he is already the heir of his father's promise (Galatians 4:1).
3. Spiritually, the New Testament speaks of heirs of God: Christians who receive, as adopted sons, the blessings of the messianic kingdom (Romans 8:17; Galatians 3:29). To be an heir is to have a guaranteed share in divine promises.
4. Christ himself is called heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2) — not only does he reign, but he inherits the entire creation as the only Son of the Father.
G2818.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "kleros" (the lot, the portion that falls to the one who draws it) and "nemô" (to possess, to distribute). An heir is literally one to whom is assigned in share what belongs to another. In Hebrew, the word "yarash" (to possess, to inherit) often translates this notion of acquiring a family possession. The image is that of drawing lots, of the lot that becomes your property.
G2818.emploi: This word appears 14 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul's epistles and in the Epistle to the Hebrews. It is first used in the concrete sense: the heir in a legal succession (Matthew 21:38; Mark 12:7; Luke 20:14). Then it spiritualizes: Abraham is heir of God's promise (Romans 4:13-14), not by the law but by faith. Christians are heirs of the promises made to Abraham (Galatians 3:29) and even heirs with Christ of the glory of God (Romans 8:17). The Epistle to the Hebrews also applies it to the patriarchs who received divine promises (Hebrews 6:17; 11:7). The meaning thus focuses on the notion of possession guaranteed by a promise or an acquired right.
G2818.portee: For the believer, this word affirms a fundamental truth: we are not merely servants, but sons, and therefore heirs (Galatians 4:7). This changes everything: God's promises are not a favor he could withdraw, but an inheritance that legally belongs to us by adoption in Christ. It is a source of unwavering confidence in the Christian life. At the same time, recognizing Christ as heir of all things reminds us of his absolute lordship and our dependence on him.

sens: object drawn at random to decide something
result of the drawing, what falls to someone
share, portion, inheritance
charge, responsibility entrusted
G2819.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the physical object that is thrown or drawn to make a decision at random. When there is no agreement, one "draws lots": this is how the soldiers divided Jesus' garments at the cross (Matthew 27:35, Mark 15:24, Luke 23:34, John 19:24).
2. By extension, it refers to the result of the drawing, what falls to someone through this process. After casting lots to appoint an apostle in place of Judas, "the lot fell on Matthias" (Acts 1:26).
3. The word takes on a broader meaning: it designates the share or inheritance one receives, whether obtained by drawing lots or not. Peter speaks of Judas' "share in the ministry" (Acts 1:17), and Paul writes to the Colossians that they have been made "worthy to share in the inheritance [of the Lord]" (Colossians 1:12).
4. It can also signify the charge or responsibility that has been received — what the apostles call their "ministry." It is the lot entrusted, the mission that must be accomplished.
G2819.origine: The Greek word klēros comes from a root that evokes the idea of sharing and destination. In Hebrew, the main corresponding word is gôrāl ("lot, drawing lots"), which refers to the pebble or object that was drawn to make a decision. In the Greek Old Testament, klēros also translates nāḥălāh ("inheritance"), which explains why the word comes to mean not only the drawing itself but also the share that one obtains — the inheritance that is assigned to you.
G2819.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. First, the four Passion accounts use "lot" for the sharing of Jesus' garments (Matthew 27:35, Mark 15:24, Luke 23:34, John 19:24): this is the concrete sense of drawing lots. Then, Acts uses it for the drawing that designates Matthias (Acts 1:26) and to speak of Judas' "share" in the ministry (Acts 1:17). Finally, Paul uses it figuratively to designate our share in the Kingdom of God and the inheritance that God reserves for us in Christ (Colossians 1:12, Acts 26:18): it is a share of honor, a glorious destiny. Peter uses it for the pastoral charges entrusted to the elders (1 Peter 5:3).
G2819.portee: This word reminds the believer that our life in Christ is not the result of chance: our place in the Church, our ministry, our eternal inheritance are assigned to us by God Himself, far beyond any drawing of lots. While the soldiers saw in Jesus' garments only a booty to be shared by lot, Scripture sees the fulfillment of God's plan. We have received a "lot" — a destiny, a glorious share — which is our calling in Christ.

sens: Receive a share as an inheritance by drawing lots
Be designated by the lot to possess something
Be assigned a portion or inheritance
G2820.detail:
1. The word first evokes the action of drawing lots to distribute an inheritance: in the Old Testament, lots were drawn to divide the lands among the tribes of Israel. This is the primitive, concrete sense of the verb.
2. More broadly, it means to be chosen by the lot, thus being designated to receive something. The lot, in the Bible, expresses the will of God: the one designated by the lot is the one chosen by God.
3. In Ephesians 1:11, Paul uses it figuratively: believers have become "heirs," meaning they have been assigned, by divine will, a share in the promised inheritance. God has predestined them to receive this inheritance as a guaranteed possession.
G2820.origine: The word comes from the Greek root κλῆρος (klêros), which means "lot," "drawing lots," "portion obtained by the lot." This noun κλῆρος itself is very ancient and common in the Greek Bible to designate an inheritance divided by drawing lots. The verb κληρόω is its verbal form: "to draw lots" or "to give by the lot." The practice of drawing lots to divide the lands is attested in the Old Testament, notably in the book of Joshua.
G2820.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 1:11. Paul uses it in the passive voice to describe the status of believers: "we have been assigned (as an inheritance)." The context is that of predestination and grace: God, by His sovereign will, has designated believers to be heirs of the promise. Paul chooses this rare verb to emphasize that our status as heirs is not the result of chance or our merits, but of God's predetermined purpose, like a portion assigned by divine drawing lots.
G2820.portee: This word reminds the Christian that his status as an heir of God is not an accident or a reward he has earned: it is an act of divine predestination, a sovereign choice of God inscribed in advance. The believer can therefore find assurance and gratitude in knowing that his eternal inheritance is guaranteed, not by his own strength, but by the settled counsel of divine will.

sens: the act of calling someone to a function or condition
the divine invitation to enter into a saving relationship with God
the condition or status in which someone finds themselves at the time of this call
the hope and reward attached to this divine call
the manner of living worthy of one who has received this call
G2821.detail:
1. Calling primarily refers to the act of calling, the invitation addressed to someone. It is God who calls believers to Himself, as in Romans 11:29 where Paul speaks of "the calling" of God, which is irrevocable and without repentance.

2. This word takes on its strongest meaning when it designates the divine call to salvation itself. In Ephesians 1:18, Paul prays that the eyes of the heart may be enlightened so that the reader may know "the hope to which He has called you" — it is the hope of salvation in Christ.

3. The word also means the condition or situation in which one was when God called us. In 1 Corinthians 7:20, Paul says: "Let each one remain in the condition in which he was called." He speaks here of one's civil, family, or professional condition.

4. The calling includes the richness of what God promises us: in Ephesians 1:18, it is accompanied by a "hope" and a "glory" of inheritance that God reserves for the saints.

5. The calling also commits the believer to a manner of living: in Ephesians 4:1, Paul exhorts to "walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called," which means that our life must reflect the greatness of the divine call received.
G2821.origine: The word κλῆσις comes from the verb καλέω (kaléô), which means "to call." It is the call of God that constitutes the heart of the word: not an ordinary human call, but the sovereign invitation of the living God. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew word קָרָא (qârâ), which also means "to call." The family of this Greek word also includes the noun κλητός (klêtos), "called," which designates one who has received the divine call, and the verb κάλεμα, from which our word derives.
G2821.emploi: The word κλῆσις appears 11 times in the New Testament, always in relation to the divine call. Paul frequently uses it to speak of the call to salvation in Christ (Romans 11:29; 1 Corinthians 1:26; Ephesians 1:18, 4:1, 4; Philippians 3:14). In 1 Corinthians 7:20, it takes on a more specific meaning: the condition or social state in which one was living when God called us. The later epistles (2 Timothy 1:9, Hebrews 3:1, 2 Peter 1:10) retain this sense of the divine call to salvation, while 2 Thessalonians 1:11 speaks of being "counted worthy of the calling." In all uses, it is always God who calls, never man.
G2821.portee: Understanding one's Christian calling means recognizing that our conversion is not a purely personal decision: it is God who has called us. This calling is not without consequence — it commits us to walk worthily, that is, to live in a manner consistent with the greatness and holiness of the One who has called us. It is also a source of certain hope, for it is God Himself who has made this call and who maintains it.

sens: who has received a call, a summons
who has been chosen by God for a function or mission
who has been elected by God for salvation
holy by divine vocation
G2822.detail:
1. In the concrete and ancient sense, the word refers to someone who has received an invitation or a call: one thinks of a guest invited to a feast. But in the New Testament, this sense disappears in favor of the religious meaning.

2. The word first applies to one whom God calls to a specific function, particularly to the apostleship: Paul presents himself as "called to be an apostle" (Romans 1:1, 1 Corinthians 1:1), meaning that God entrusted him with this mission.

3. More broadly, the word designates all believers whom God calls to salvation: "those who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28) are the Christians whom God intended to save. It is a personal vocation from the Lord.

4. Finally, "called saints" (Romans 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:2) summarizes the two ideas: believers are sanctified, set apart for God, because God has called them. The passage in Matthew 22:14 ("many are called, but few are chosen") suggests that being called is a privilege, but that the final election belongs to God alone.
G2822.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to call" (kalèô). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the terms "to cry, to call" (qara) and "call, convocation" (miqra) correspond to this semantic field. The basic image is that of a voice calling someone: God speaks and his people respond. For the Greeks, a "called one" was primarily someone invited to a feast; Christian authors adopted this form of adjective to express the idea of divine vocation.
G2822.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, only in the letters of Paul, in the epistle of Jude, and in Revelation. Paul uses it to describe himself as an apostle (Romans 1:1, 1 Corinthians 1:1), but also to speak of all believers: they are the "called ones" by Jesus Christ or according to God's purpose (Romans 1:6, Romans 8:28). In 1 Corinthians 1:24, the "called ones" receive the riches of Christ. In Matthew (22:14), the popular saying "many are called, few are chosen" plays on the difference between those who have received the invitation and those whom God has definitively chosen. Revelation (17:14) adds to this distinction: the "called, chosen, and faithful" form the elite of believers. In 1 Corinthians 1:2, the saints are defined by this divine vocation.
G2822.portee: This word reminds the reader that their faith is not the result of chance or solely their own will: it is God who calls. For Paul and for every believer, being "called" means that God has had a plan for us and has personally addressed us. This gives dignity to the Christian life — they are not a lost soul, but someone whom the Lord has designated and chosen. Conversely, being called requires a faithful response and real sanctification: it is not a cheap or passive distinction, but the beginning of a dedicated life.

sens: oven or furnace used for baking bread or melting metals
action of throwing something into the fire to destroy it
G2823.detail:
1. The oven is a container or structure made of clay used for baking bread and melting metals. In Israel, it was a common element of daily life, either domestic or communal. Jesus uses it to evoke fragility and destiny: "the grass of the fields, which exists today and tomorrow will be thrown into the oven" (Matthew 6:30).
2. By extension, "to throw into the oven" means to destroy, eliminate by fire. This image symbolizes judgment or annihilation: the fire of the oven consumes and reduces to nothing what is thrown into it. The same expression appears in Luke 12:28, where Jesus uses it to teach trust in God despite our fears.
G2823.origine: The Greek word κλίβανος comes from an ancient root and has Greek variants (notably κρίβ- in Attic). In Hebrew, it corresponds to תַּנּוּר (tannur), which also designates an oven or furnace. This word is rooted in the material vocabulary of the ancient Near East: any oven intended to transform by fire.
G2823.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, only in Matthew (6:30) and Luke (12:28), in two identical logia of Jesus. In these two parallel passages, Jesus speaks of the grass that God adorns with beauty but which will be "thrown into the oven" tomorrow. This is not a technical description of the oven, but an image of transience and judgment. The ephemeral grass, although adorned with temporal glory, is destined to be consumed. This comparison serves to teach the absurdity of material worry: if God cares for such ephemeral things, how much more will he care for us.
G2823.portee: This image of the oven reveals Jesus' teaching on the relative value of earthly goods and the hierarchy of concerns. It invites the believer to detach their heart from fragile and perishable things, and to trust God for what is necessary. The oven symbolizes divine judgment regarding what does not last: it is an invitation to seek first the kingdom of God.

sens: Geographical area, region, territory
Delimited space of a certain extent
G2824.detail:
1. The word designates a region, a country in the sense of a relatively large geographical area. Paul speaks of the "regions" of Achaia (2 Corinthians 11:10) or of Syria and Cilicia (Galatians 1:21): these are not specific cities, but territories, regional spaces where he has worked or intends to go. The word evokes the idea of extent and limit: a region has borders, it encompasses several places.
2. By extension, the word can evoke inclination or slope — the original image of ancient Greek — but in the New Testament, only the sense of region, of delimited space, is retained. In Romans 15:23, Paul has completed his apostolic work in these Mediterranean regions, and he now wants to go to Rome.
G2824.origine: The word comes from the verb "to lean" or "to incline" (κλίνω). Initially, it designated a slope, an inclination of the terrain — notably from north to the equator, in ancient geography. The meaning has broadened to designate a region, an area of land, as if speaking of an "inclined zone" or a "band of territory." This is how the Hebrew פִּנָּה (corner, angle) could be translated by this term in ancient Greek.
G2824.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the plural and always in Paul's epistles. In Romans 15:23, Paul says that he has nothing that holds him in these regions — he speaks of the entire Mediterranean basin where he has already worked (North Africa, Greece, Asia Minor). In 2 Corinthians 11:10, he mentions the regions of Achaia, the Greek region where the assembly of Corinth is established. In Galatians 1:21, he mentions the regions of Syria and Cilicia, where he stayed after his conversion. In all cases, the word serves to designate a wide area of land, an identified geographical space.
G2824.portee: This word reminds us that the apostle Paul had a broad geographical vision of his ministry: he did not think in terms of isolated cities, but of entire regions to evangelize. This shows the scope and apostolic ambition of the first Christian century, as well as the awareness that the Good News was to spread over vast territories. It is also a reminder that the Gospel is never limited to a single place, but spreads from region to region.

sens: piece of furniture for resting on which one lies down to sleep or rest
improvised stretcher or litter for transporting a sick person
object placed under or on which something is stored
marital bed, matrimonial bed
G2825.detail:
1. The bed is the main piece of furniture in the room where one sleeps and rests: it is a common item of household furniture. Matthew 9:2 shows people bringing a paralytic lying on a bed to present him to Jesus, indicating that the bed was portable enough to be carried.
2. By extension, the word also refers to the improvised stretcher on which sick people were transported: the paralytic in Luke 5:18 is carried on a bed to be brought before Jesus, showing that the bed could serve as a litter.
3. The word can also refer to the place where things are stored, as in Mark 4:21, where a lamp should not be placed under the bed (that is, hidden), but on the lampstand to shine.
4. In a figurative or marital sense, the bed represents marriage and marital life (Revelation 2:22), where adultery lies with its partners.
G2825.origine: The word comes from the Greek κλίνω (klínō), which means "to incline" or "to lean." The bed is therefore etymologically the place where one inclines, lies down, and rests one's body. In Hebrew, the word מִטָּה (mittâ) that κλίνη translates in the Greek Old Testament refers to both domestic beds and stretchers or litters.
G2825.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Synoptic Gospels. It first describes the bed as a piece of furniture for resting: the place where people sleep (Luke 8:16, Luke 17:34). It frequently appears in miracle and healing scenes where the sick are carried on their bed to Jesus (Matthew 9:2, 9:6; Mark 7:30; Luke 5:18), showing that the bed was light enough to be transported. Mark 4:21 uses it in a metaphorical sense: the lamp should not be placed under the bed, that is, hidden. Once in Mark 7:4, the word is translated as "brass" (copper or bronze), which seems to be a textual error or an ancient variant. Finally, Revelation 2:22 uses it in the sense of a marital bed.
G2825.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus is concerned with the concrete lives of people, even in their most humble needs: sleeping, resting, being healed from illness. The scenes where paralytics are carried on their bed to Jesus show the importance of practical faith: the community mobilizes to bring the sick person. It is also a call to transparency: the lamp should not remain hidden under the bed, but shine. For the Christian, this suggests that faith should not be concealed, but manifested.

sens: small bed or mattress
stretcher or litter for transporting a sick person
G2826.detail:
1. This word refers to a small bed, probably a mattress or simple bedding, the type of bed a poor person or sick person would use in the first century. It is a diminutive of the Greek κλίνη ("bed"), which marks the humility and modesty of the object — not a magnificent bed, but a humble sleeping place. In Luke 5:19, friends lower a paralyzed man "with his bed" through the roof to Jesus: this bed was light and portable.
2. Here, the bed primarily functions as a stretcher or litter on which a sick person is transported. The paralyzed man lay immobile on it, and his friends lowered him lying on it. After the healing, Jesus commands him (Luke 5:24) to "take up his bed" — that is, to lift what was carrying him — and walk: the bed thus becomes a sign of his past helplessness and regained strength.
G2826.origine: It is a diminutive Greek word of κλίνη ("bed"). The diminutive creates a nuance of intimacy or modesty: not a grand bed of the rich, but a humble sleeping place. The word expresses the image of a resting surface — something that can be lowered, carried, taken, and removed. It is a common term in everyday Greek of the first century.
G2826.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke, in the account of the paralytic (Luke 5:19, 24). In both occurrences, the context is identical: the bed is the object that carries a sick man, transported by others, then used by him to manifest his healing. In Luke, who writes for a Greek audience, this simple little word vividly depicts the misery of the infirm and the solidarity of his friends who lower him to Jesus.
G2826.portee: This small bed tells of friendship, faith, and healing. It reminds us that those who cannot come to Jesus on their own are carried by the intercession and love of their loved ones. And when Jesus commands the paralytic to take up his bed and walk, it is an invitation to no longer be carried, to rise, to reclaim a standing and free life. For the reader, this bed is the image of all that paralyzes us and that Jesus can transform.

sens: To bend, incline downward (a part of the body)
To lay down, rest (the head)
To decrease, diminish (of light, day)
To turn to flee (figuratively, for troops)
G2827.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of bending or inclining something downward. Jesus "bows" his head at the moment of death (John 19:30), the ultimate gesture of submission. The women at the tomb "bow" their faces to the ground, overwhelmed with terror (Luke 24:5).

2. To lay down or rest one's head somewhere, especially for sleeping. Jesus says he has "nowhere to lay his head" (Matthew 8:20), describing his complete destitution: no home, no bed, no stability.

3. The day that "declines" or goes away: the sun sets on the horizon, the light fades (Luke 24:29). It is the evening, the moment when night approaches.

4. Figuratively, soldiers who "turn to flee" "bend" backward to escape from battle (Hebrews 11:34). It is an image of forced retreat.
G2827.origine: This Greek verb comes from a root that evokes the action of folding, bending, or curving. It appears mainly in the Greek translation of the Old Testament to render the Hebrew "נָטָה" (nâtâh), which means to extend, incline, or turn. The family of the word also includes nouns designating a bed or a support. It is a simple and visual term, rooted in the gesture of the body.
G2827.emploi: The verb appears seven times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke. It first describes the physical gesture of bending the head: Jesus bows it in dying (John 19:30), the women bow it in fear (Luke 24:5). It then denotes rest: Jesus has "nowhere to lay his head" (Matthew 8:20, Luke 9:58), an image of his destitution and lack of earthly anchorage. It also expresses the decline of the day, the transition from day to night (Luke 9:12, Luke 24:29). Once it is used in a figurative and military sense: troops that "turn to flee" (Hebrews 11:34). The meaning varies little: it is always a movement downward, crumbling, or retreat.
G2827.portee: This word reveals the condition of Jesus and his humility: he has nowhere to lay his head, he bows his head in the face of death. For the believer, "to bend" the head is also a gesture of surrender and trust. The decline of the day reminds us of the brevity of earthly time and the urgency of welcoming the Lord (the disciples urge Jesus: "stay with us, for the evening is approaching").

sens: A group of people sitting or lying together, organized in a line or row
An arrangement set up for several people to stand side by side or rest collectively
G2828.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a place where one lies down or stretches out: a bed, a couch, a bench. However, in the New Testament, it takes on a collective meaning: it refers to a group of people who are sitting or lying next to each other, forming a line or row. 2. In the account of Luke 9:14, Jesus asks his disciples to have the five thousand men sit in "rows" of fifty. This illustrates how people are organized into distinct groups, each forming a compact unit. It is a practical and orderly way to present the crowds for a meal or food distribution.
G2828.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to lean, to bow, to lie down." The initial idea is of someone lying down or stretching out on a bed or piece of furniture. From there, the word first designated the furniture itself (bed, couch), and then by extension, a group of people arranged in such a way as to form a coherent line, as if they were lying down together.
G2828.emploi: This word appears only once in the Gospels: in Luke 9:14, during the feeding of the five thousand. Jesus commands his disciples to have the crowd sit in rows of fifty men. The choice of this term emphasizes the organization and order that Jesus imposes within a chaotic crowd, thus allowing everyone to be fed in a fair and methodical manner. It is a concrete detail that shows the practical wisdom of the Lord in the face of logistical challenges.
G2828.portee: This word reminds us that even in the face of immense crowds and complex situations, God values order and organization. For the reader, it highlights how Jesus does not merely perform a miracle: he establishes a fair and orderly distribution, showing that faith does not exclude prudence and practical planning. It is a lesson for church leaders and those who organize the community.

sens: The act of stealing, taking secretly what belongs to another
Figuratively: injustice, crime against one's neighbor
G2829.detail:
1. Theft is the act of secretly or forcibly taking what belongs to someone else — it is larceny, a crime. Jesus lists theft among the evils that defile the human heart, alongside murder and adultery (Matthew 15:19).
2. Figuratively, theft symbolizes injustice and disregard for the rights of others: it is an infringement upon one's neighbor. Mark 7:21 also places theft in the list of evil thoughts that spring from a corrupt heart.
G2829.origine: The Greek word κλοπή comes from the verb κλέπτω (kleptō), "to steal," which means to take secretly or furtively. The root evokes the idea of subtraction, of taking away. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses גָּנַב (ganav) to denote the same act: to steal, to take away.
G2829.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in lists of sins enumerated by Jesus. In Matthew 15:19 and Mark 7:21, it is included among the "evil thoughts" or "fornications" that defile a person from within. These two parallel passages show that Jesus categorizes theft not only among material crimes but among the evils that emerge from an unpurified heart. The lists are nearly identical in both Gospels, underscoring Jesus' teaching: theft comes from the heart.
G2829.portee: This teaching of Jesus reminds the believer that theft is not merely an external transgression: it reveals a selfish and unjust heart. Recognizing theft as an evil thought means accepting that our nature needs transformation. It is a call to righteousness not only in actions but in the intentions of the heart.

sens: Wave, surge of the sea
Agitation, tumultuous movement of the waters
Instability, moral or spiritual inconsistency
G2830.detail:
1. A wave is a large swell or powerful movement of water raised by a storm. When Jesus calms the storm in Luke 8:24, he "rebukes the wind and the waves" to calm them — the word refers to those unleashed masses of water that threaten the boat.
2. The wave evokes chaotic agitation, the tumult of waters pushed in all directions. In James 1:6, the man who doubts is compared to "a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind": the image shows something unstable, without a fixed direction.
3. By spiritual extension, the wave symbolizes inconsistency and moral instability: doubt causes the believer to waver like the wave oscillates under the wind, without a firm grip on faith.
G2830.origine: The Greek word comes from a root evoking the movement of water that submerges or envelops. Its close relative is κῦμα (kyma, "wave"), which also designates a wave, but κλύδων emphasizes the violent and tumultuous nature, the crashing wave rather than the regular swell. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates סַעַר (storm, turmoil), showing that the word carries the idea of chaos and danger.
G2830.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 8:24, it describes the threatening waves of the Sea of Galilee that Jesus calms by his divine authority — a context of miracle and deliverance. In James 1:6, it becomes a moral image: the man who prays without faith is unstable like a wave shaken by the wind, unable to receive what he asks for. Both uses play on instability: physical and material on one side, spiritual and moral on the other.
G2830.portee: This word helps the believer understand two truths: first, that Jesus alone masters the chaotic and dangerous forces of this world — even the sea obeys him. Second, that authentic faith is the opposite of doubt; to doubt is to be tossed about like a wave, without a stable foundation. For the reader, the contrast teaches the importance of asking with complete trust, anchored in God.

sens: Being shaken, agitated by the waves
Being tossed about in every direction, without stability
Being unstable in thought, convictions
G2831.detail:
1. The word first describes the violent movement of a boat tossed by the waves of the sea — a very concrete image of physical instability (Isaiah 57:20 thus evokes the waves of the sea that cannot rest).
2. Figuratively, it denotes moral or spiritual instability: to be "floating" is to be carried to and fro, without a stable direction. Paul uses this term in Ephesians 4:14 to describe immature Christians who are not firmly anchored in faith and who are led astray like ships without a rudder.
3. This instability is particularly expressed by vulnerability to false doctrines: the "floating" Christian lacks spiritual foundations and is rocked by the deceptive winds of every new teaching contrary to the truth.
G2831.origine: The word comes from the root κλύδων (klúdōn), which means "wave" or "flow of the sea." It is an ancient Greek term that paints the image of the chaotic and unpredictable movement of waters. The verbal form adds the sense of "being shaken by": one is not an actor, but passive, tossed about. In Hebrew, this same sense of being agitated or pushed away is rendered by גָּרַשׁ (garach).
G2831.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 4:14. Paul uses it to warn the Christians of Colossae (and more broadly all believers) against spiritual immaturity. He urges them to no longer be "children tossed to and fro," that is, wavering, inconsistent in faith. The context shows that this instability is dangerous: it exposes the believer to the seduction of false teachings, to the cunning of those who seek to mislead. The term underscores the importance of spiritual growth and being rooted in the knowledge of Christ to gain unshakeable stability.
G2831.portee: For the Christian, this word invites introspection: am I firmly anchored in my faith, or am I "floating," vulnerable to the winds of doctrine that blow around me? It is a call to grow spiritually, to study the Word, to let the truth of the Gospel root us. Growing means moving from instability to firmness, from dependence on every new influence to a stable conviction in Christ.

sens: man whose wife Mary was present at the foot of the cross of Jesus
G2832.detail: Clopas is a man whose wife, also named Mary, was at the foot of the cross during the crucifixion of Jesus (John 19:25). He appears only once in the Gospels, and only as an identifier of this faithful woman.
G2832.origine: The name Clopas is of Aramaic origin, the mother tongue spoken by Jesus and the early disciples. It is a name given to a Jewish man of the time, likely a disciple or someone close to Jesus' circle, but we have only this brief mention to know him.
G2832.emploi: Clopas appears only once in the Gospel of John (19:25), in the crucial scene where John lists the women present at Jesus' death. He is named only because his wife Mary was one of those women who followed Jesus to the end. This shows that some close to the Lord, whose names remain largely unknown to us, participated in the story of the passion.
G2832.portee: The mention of Clopas reminds us that the cross gathered a small group of faithful — mostly women — who had the courage to remain while the disciples fled. These seemingly insignificant figures in the Gospel narrative participated in the most important moments of Jesus' life, encouraging the reader to see that silent faithfulness is valued in the eyes of God.

sens: To have a tingling or irritating sensation on the skin that makes one want to scratch
Figuratively, to have an intense and irrepressible desire, a craving that tickles the mind
G2833.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to itch means to feel that unpleasant tingling sensation on the skin that provokes the urge to scratch. It is a surface irritation, a bodily itch.
2. Paul uses it figuratively in 2 Timothy 4:3 to describe a mental craving: that of 'hearing pleasant things.' Itching ears represent a fervent and capricious desire for immediate pleasure, a craving that cannot be restrained, just as one cannot help but scratch an itch. It is a thirst for spiritual entertainment rather than solid truth.
G2833.origine: The word κνήθω is a late form of the verb κνάω, which literally means to scratch or rub. The image comes from the body and its sensations: this visceral need felt when one is irritated. The word describes an involuntary and persistent sensation, difficult to ignore.
G2833.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:3, in the passive and future ('they will have itching ears'). Paul uses it to characterize the spiritual attitude of those who will soon reject sound doctrine: instead of accepting true teaching, even demanding, they will want words that tickle their ears and flatter their inclinations. The word vividly paints this inability to endure what tires or disturbs, this desire for spiritual comfort at all costs.
G2833.portee: This word invites the Christian to examine themselves: am I not like those men with itching ears, seeking primarily to be reassured or entertained rather than transformed by the truth? It calls for vigilance against the allure of sweet and easy messages that demand nothing. True faith is built on solidity, not comfort.

sens: City and peninsula on the southwest coast of Asia Minor
G2834.detail: Cnidus is an important port city located at the southwestern tip of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). It was a well-known maritime landmark in antiquity. In Acts 27:7, Paul and his companions, on their way to Rome, reach the vicinity of Cnidus but are prevented from landing by contrary winds, forcing them to continue their navigation toward Crete.
G2834.origine: The Greek name Κνίδος (Knidos) refers to this famous Greek port city, established as a major commercial and cultural center of the ancient Mediterranean world. The city was renowned for its shipbuilding and maritime trade.
G2834.emploi: Cnidus appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:7, during the account of Paul's journey to Rome. This is a practical geographical mention: Luke, the author of Acts, notes the position of this port to situate the boat's route and explain the obstacles encountered during this perilous crossing toward the West.

sens: Small Roman coin worth a quarter of an as
More generally, the smallest coin, symbol of extreme poverty
G2835.detail:
1. The quadrant is a Roman coin of very low value, equivalent to a quarter of an as (the as itself being a low-value bronze coin). It is a tiny monetary unit in the Roman system. In Matthew 5:26, Jesus mentions it to describe the last small debt that must be paid: 'you will not get out of there until you have paid the last quadrant.'
2. More broadly, the word symbolizes extreme poverty and what is smallest in terms of material goods. In Mark 12:42, the poor widow puts only two small quadrants (or two small coins) into the treasury, representing all she has and demonstrating her total destitution.
G2835.origine: The word κοδράντης comes directly from the Latin quadrans, which literally means 'quarter' (from quadrum, square). The Gospels borrowed this Latin term because it was a real currency circulating in Palestine at the time of Rome. The Greek word faithfully reproduces the Latin pronunciation and retains the idea of division into four parts.
G2835.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Gospels. In Matthew 5:26, in the context of judgment and reconciliation, Jesus teaches that one must settle even the smallest debts (the last quadrant). In Mark 12:42, during the episode of the widow who puts her offering into the temple treasury, the quadrant denotes the smallest currency, the minimal alms of a woman reduced to poverty. In both cases, the word emphasizes the idea of totality — paying down to the last coin, or giving up to the last cent one possesses.
G2835.portee: The quadrant reminds the reader that nothing escapes God's notice, not even the smallest thing: no debt, no secret, no act of mercy is too insignificant for His attention. This coin also symbolizes the value that God places on the poorest and the humblest; the widow who gives her two quadrants is praised by Jesus because she has given all she had, while the rich have only given from their surplus. It is an invitation to generosity without calculation and an awareness that God weighs our actions according to the heart, not according to quantity.

sens: The belly or stomach, part of the body where digestion occurs
The uterus or the belly of a pregnant mother
