That which nourishes or sustains
The inner self, heart, or deep thoughts
G2836.detail: 1. The belly refers to the part of the human body containing the stomach and intestines. Mark 7:19 shows how food first enters the belly before being expelled. Romans 16:18 speaks of servants "whose god is their belly," meaning their carnal appetites are their god. 2. The maternal breast refers to the uterus, the place where the child forms and develops before birth. Luke 1:42 speaks of "the fruit of your womb" referring to Jesus carried by Mary while pregnant. John 3:4 recounts Nicodemus's question: how can a man "enter his mother's womb" to be born again? 3. Speaking of sustenance, John 7:38 uses "belly" symbolically, as a source of life and blessing that flows. Luke 15:16 shows a hungry person longing to fill his belly, an expression of his destitution. 4. Figuratively, the belly can signify the deep inner self, hidden thoughts, what is at the heart of a person, as in Hebrew expressions that equate the belly with the seat of emotions and intentions.
G2836.origine: The Greek word koilia comes from koilos ("hollow, empty"), which evokes the hollow space of the body. In Hebrew, it primarily translates beten ("belly"), meeh ("entrails"), qerev ("inner"), and also rechem ("uterus"). These Hebrew words emphasize that the belly is the place of physical digestion, but also, in biblical thought, the seat of deep feelings and intentions — where emotions and hidden thoughts reside, even before the heart.
G2836.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the New Testament. In the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke), it is used notably to describe bodily phenomena: digestion (Mark 7:19), hunger (Luke 15:16), or the present inability at birth (Acts 14:8). The usage concerning maternity is very frequent in Luke (1:41-42, 2:21, 11:27, 23:29), which emphasizes the conception and gestation of Jesus and John the Baptist. Paul uses the word critically: Philippians 3:19 denounces those whose "god is their belly" (that is, the fulfillment of carnal desires), while 1 Corinthians 6:13 asserts that "foods are for the belly, and the belly for foods," but reminds that the believer's body is much more than that. Revelation 10:9-10 uses the word symbolically: the little book swallowed in the seer's belly tastes sweet in the mouth but becomes bitter in the belly.
G2836.portee: For the believer, this word reminds of the incarnation: Jesus truly took on a body, grew in the womb of Mary, and was truly human. It also invites us to examine what fills our "belly" in a broader sense — our appetites, our secret desires — and to ask whether it is Christ who reigns in us or our cravings. John 7:38 promises that whoever believes will have rivers of living water flowing from his belly: an image of the inner transformation that the Holy Spirit works in the believer.

sens: To close one's eyes and rest the body in sleep
To be asleep, dozing
To be dead, deceased (figurative and spiritual sense)
G2837.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of natural sleep: closing one's eyes and resting. It is the state of physical rest, like Peter who slept between two soldiers despite being chained (Acts 12:6), or the disciples dozing while Jesus prayed (Luke 22:45).
2. Sometimes the word refers to the state of one who falls asleep or begins to doze, close to deep sleep.
3. In the New Testament, this word takes on a very special figurative meaning: it designates the death of believers. Jesus says of Lazarus, "our friend sleeps" when he is dead (John 11:11). Paul speaks of those "who have died" by saying "those who sleep in Jesus" (1 Thessalonians 4:14). This language expresses that for a Christian, death is not a definitive end but a sleep from which he will awaken at the resurrection — a way of saying that death is conquered by faith in Christ.
G2837.origine: The Greek verb κοιμάω comes from a root that evokes the idea of lying down, resting. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the word שָׁכַב (shakav), which literally means "to lie down" or "to rest," is often translated by this verb in the Greek version. The word belongs to a family of terms denoting rest and lying down of the body. This is why the metaphor of sleep to speak of death was natural: the dead are said to "rest" or "sleep" as if the body had lain down for eternity.
G2837.emploi: This verb appears 18 times in the New Testament. In the literal sense, it describes natural sleep: Peter was sleeping in prison (Acts 12:6), the disciples were falling asleep during prayer (Luke 22:45). But most of its uses are metaphorical: Paul regularly uses it to denote the death of believers (1 Corinthians 15:6, 15:18, 15:20; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-15). This metaphor is specifically Christian — it expresses the hope that death is not definitive for those who believe in Christ. In other uses, the word describes the state of drowsiness or half-sleep (John 11:12). The source definition notes that the middle and passive (reflexive forms) mean "to fall asleep" or "to be asleep," while the metaphorical passive means "to die."
G2837.portee: This word opens up a new perspective on death for the believer. Instead of speaking of "end" or "nothingness," the New Testament chooses the image of sleep — which suggests rest, peace, and above all, the expectation of awakening. This says something essential: for the Christian, death is a temporary passage, not a final break. Paul draws practical comfort from this for the Thessalonians grieving over the death of their brothers: since they sleep, they will rise again (1 Thessalonians 4:14). It is a language of hope that transforms our fear of dying.

sens: State of light rest or natural sleep
Sleep or rest considered as a transition, a passage
Figuratively: death, viewed as a rest (death of the believer)
G2838.detail:
1. Drowsiness refers to the state of one who falls asleep or begins to sleep — this light and natural state of sleep. It is the rest of the body that ceases its activities. In John 11:13, the disciples think that Jesus is speaking of the ordinary sleep of Lazarus, of his natural rest.

2. The word can also evoke the idea of rest or transition, that of a passage to another state. This is why it fits well with the biblical image of sleep as an intermediate rest.

3. For the believer, death can be described as drowsiness, not because it is not real, but because it is a rest before the resurrection. It is a soothing and hopeful way to speak of death — the body sleeps in anticipation of its eternal awakening.
G2838.origine: The word comes from the root κοιμάω which means "to lie down, to fall asleep, to sleep." Drowsiness is thus the action or state of falling asleep, the rest of sleep. It is a compound word that designates the state rather than the action. In the Greek language, this term retains a softness that makes it appropriate when speaking of the death of the believer as a rest.
G2838.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 11:13. In this passage, Jesus tells his disciples that Lazarus is dead using the image of sleep: "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep." The disciples understand him literally, thinking of an ordinary drowsiness, a physical rest that would do good to the sick man. Jesus then has to clarify his thought by saying openly: "Lazarus is dead." This misunderstanding between the image (sleep) and the reality (death) shows how the word served to gently veil a difficult truth.
G2838.portee: This word invites the believer to consider death not as a definitive end, but as a temporary rest awaiting resurrection. The image of sleep expresses God's tenderness towards His children and the Christian hope: death is not nothingness, but a drowsiness from which one will awaken. It calms fear and discreetly affirms faith in eternal life.

sens: that which is common, ordinary, shared by all
that which is not consecrated, that has not been set apart for God
that which ritually defiles the one who touches or consumes it
that which is considered impure by law or tradition
G2839G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what is common or ordinary, what everyone shares — the opposite of what is particular or reserved. In Acts 2:44 and 4:32, the early Christians shared everything: their possessions, their spiritual life are shared.
2. Next, "impure" describes what has not been consecrated to God, what remains in the profane realm. It is a religious term: what does not belong to God cannot enter His temple or be offered in His worship.
3. Concretely, it is that which renders a person ritually impure if they touch or consume it. Unwashed hands before a meal (Mark 7:2, 5) render one impure according to the tradition of the Pharisees. Animals declared impure by the Law — the pig, shellfish — communicate their impurity (Acts 10:14).
4. Impurity here is often a matter of perception and religious tradition. Romans 14:14 poses the key question: is something impure in itself, or only for the one who believes it to be impure? Each person's conscience plays a role in judging what defiles.
G2839G.origine: The Greek κοινός comes from a root meaning "to share" or "to be together." It is the same word found in "communion" (κοινωνία). To be common is to belong to many, not to be reserved for one. From this comes the religious meaning: what is not set apart for God remains common, ordinary, profane, thus impure in the eyes of the Law. The Greek Old Testament translates Hebrew words like חֶבֶר (companion, common) with this word.
G2839G.emploi: The word κοινός appears 8 times in the New Testament. In the early Church (Acts 2:44, 4:32), it describes the goods shared among brothers. But its most intense use is in the debate over Jewish ritual purity (Mark 7:2, 5; Acts 10 and 11; Romans 14:14). After Peter's vision in Acts 10, where he sees unclean animals descending from heaven, the meaning of "impure" transforms: God teaches Peter that no man should be called "defiled" (Acts 10:28), a revolutionary change for a Jew. Romans 14:14 generalizes: it is personal conscience that determines if something is impure, not an objective rule. Hebrews 10:29 and Revelation 21:27 remind us that the defiled cannot approach God, but after the work of Christ, it is sin that defiles, not food.
G2839G.portee: This word teaches the reader that ancient ritual purity is no longer at the heart of the relationship with God. What matters is conscience, faith in Christ, and mutual respect among brothers on points where each is not yet free (Romans 14:14). The Christian discovers that God is not bound by human categories of pure and impure: His grace purifies the one who believes, beyond any external code. It is an invitation to freedom without legalism.

sens: That which belongs to many, shared
That which is ordinary, without distinction
That which is impure or profane according to the Law
G2839H.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is: that which belongs to several people at once, or that which unites a group. The early Christians in Acts 2:44 and 4:32 had everything in common, meaning they shared their possessions — the image evokes the pooling of goods. Similarly, Titus shares a common faith with Paul (Titus 1:4), meaning a faith they have in common, which unites them.
2. The word can also mean: ordinary, banal, without particular character — what is common and vulgar. This meaning develops when the word designates what is not sacred or distinguished.
3. In the religious practice of the Law, "common" takes on the meaning of impure or profane: that which has not been consecrated to God, that which is not set apart for Him. Jude 1:3 speaks of the common salvation for all believers, but this meaning of "shared" here approaches "universal."
G2839H.origine: The Greek word κοινός comes from a root meaning "together" or "to share." In Hebrew, it often translates words like אֶחָד ("one") or חֶבֶר ("associate"), which express the idea of union or bond. The Latin word communis is its direct equivalent. The basic image is that of sharing: what is common is what is possessed or done together, without distinction of private property.
G2839H.emploi: The word appears four times in the provided usages. In Acts, it first designates the pooling of goods shared by the early Christians (Acts 2:44, 4:32) — a concrete and daily act of sharing that shows the unity of the Church. In Paul (Titus 1:4), it qualifies the faith shared between a master and his disciple, marking their spiritual communion. In Jude (Jude 1:3), it extends this meaning to the salvation that is common to all believers, that is, universal and intended for the whole people. The religious context of the New Testament uses "common" to express unity and shared belonging to the body of Christ.
G2839H.portee: This word shows Christians that the Christian faith is never isolated or private: it is by nature common, shared, communal. When the early believers shared everything (Acts), it was the living expression of their common faith — a lesson on the importance of sharing and unity in the Church. The salvation announced by Jude is common to all, offered to all, reminding us that God's blessings are not reserved for a few but intended for the entire community of believers.

sens: to make impure on a ritual or spiritual level
to contaminate morally or spiritually
to declare impure
to profane what is sacred
G2840.detail:
1. To make something or someone ritually impure: this is the primary meaning of the word in Jewish laws. What is defiled can no longer be approached or used in divine worship. Jesus teaches that it is not the food that enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of it, namely bad words and thoughts (Matthew 15:11).
2. To contaminate morally or spiritually, in a broad sense: to be in contact with sin or impurity. The disciples fear becoming defiled by entering the governor's praetorium (Acts 21:28), as this would compromise their purity before God.
3. To declare or count something as impure: an act of judgment or classification. Peter learns not to count the formerly forbidden foods as defiled, since God shows him that they are now clean (Acts 10:15).
4. To profane what is holy: to remove its sacred character. The word can also refer to the act of treating a sacred reality as ordinary or impure.
G2840.origine: The word comes from κοινός (koinos), "common, ordinary," to which the verbal suffix -όω is added. Originally, "to defile" means "to make common" or "to remove the sacred character." In classical Greek, the verb expresses this idea of making ordinary. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) and the New Testament, it takes on the specific meaning of "impure according to the Law": it is a religious term that opposes "pure" (ἁγνός). The Hebrew word that the Greek defiles often translates is טמא (tamé), which means "to be impure."
G2840.emploi: The verb κοινόω appears about 14 times in the New Testament, primarily in Matthew and Mark to report Jesus' teaching on ritual purity. In Matthew 15 and Mark 7, Jesus returns six times to the idea that food does not defile a person: He thus corrects the Jewish conception of legal impurities. In Acts, the word designates different contexts: in Acts 10 and 11, Peter learns that God has purified what was once considered defiled; in Acts 21:28, he is accused of having defiled the temple by bringing in non-Jews. In Hebrews 9:13, it concerns the purifying power of sacrifices: what defiles the flesh is sanctified by ancient rituals. The word thus changes according to the context: sometimes it designates a true moral impurity, sometimes a simple legal classification that Jesus questions.
G2840.portee: This teaching of Jesus on defilement invites the Christian to look beyond legal or external purity: what truly matters is the state of the heart. Bad words, anger, hatred — what comes from within — that is what truly corrupts a person. For the believer in Christ, this revolution of the concept of purity means that the relationship with God no longer depends on ceremonial rules, but on the sincerity of the heart and obedience to God.

sens: To have a share in something, to enjoy it with others
To take an active part in a common action
To share goods or resources with someone
To associate with someone in a venture or cause
To be complicit in, to have a part in evil acts
G2841.detail:
1. To have a share in something means to share its existence or benefits. For example, in Hebrews 2:14, Christ "participates" in blood and flesh, meaning He takes part in human nature like us. It is to share something real with others.

2. Actively participating means taking a concrete part in an action. In Galatians 6:6, the one who receives instruction in the word must "share" their goods with their teacher: this is a reciprocal action, an exchange.

3. Sharing resources means giving and receiving together, especially within the community of believers. In Romans 15:27, the converted Gentiles have shared in the spiritual benefits of the Jews; therefore, they must assist them in temporal matters: this is the equity of sharing.

4. Associating with a venture or cause means entering into a communion of action. In Philippians 4:15, the church in Philippi "accounts" with Paul for the work of the Gospel: it becomes his partner.

5. Being complicit in evil acts means sharing in the responsibility for sin. In 1 Timothy 5:22, the believer must not "participate" in the sins of others: they must not associate with what is wrong, even indirectly.
G2841.origine: The word comes from the root κοινός (common, shared) and the verb ἔχω (to have, to possess). It literally means "to have in common" or "to have a common share." The family of the word includes κοινωνία (communion, sharing, association) and κοινωνός (companion, associate). In the Greek of the Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew חָבַר (to be united, to associate with), which also evokes the idea of binding together things or people.
G2841.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's epistles. It primarily describes the sharing of spiritual and material goods among believers: the Gentiles share in the spiritual benefits of Israel (Romans 15:27) and must therefore share their goods with brothers in need (Romans 12:13). It also expresses association with a cause: the Philippians "account" with Paul in the work of the Gospel (Philippians 4:15). The word can also express undesirable participation: not participating in the sins of others (1 Timothy 5:22) or in wickedness (2 John 11). In Hebrews 2:14, Jesus "participates" in flesh and blood to be able to save us. The fundamental meaning remains that of real sharing: not a distant sympathy, but a concrete pooling together.
G2841.portee: This word reveals the essence of the Christian life: it is deeply communal and supportive. Participating in spiritual goods engages one to share material goods; participating in a common cause requires commitment and sacrifice. But the word also warns: not participating in what is evil protects our purity. By seeing Jesus "participate" in our humanity, we understand that God did not keep His distance: He truly associated Himself with our condition to save us.

sens: Close sharing, intimate association between two or more people
Common participation in something sacred or spiritual
Fraternal solidarity in faith and the practice of the Gospel
Material contribution, gift offered out of fraternal solidarity
G2842.detail:
1. Communion primarily describes the close bond that unites believers with each other or with God and Christ. It is a shared intimacy, as when Paul speaks of the "communion of His Son" (1 Corinthians 1:9): being called to this communion means being admitted into a deep personal relationship with Jesus Himself.
2. The word also designates common participation in spiritual realities or sacred experiences. When Paul speaks of the "communion of His sufferings" (Philippians 3:10), it involves actively sharing what Christ endured — not just knowing it intellectually, but experiencing it within oneself. Similarly, participating in the bread and wine "is the communion of the body and blood of Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:16).
3. In the life of the Church, communion is the concrete brotherhood of believers: the fraternal communion mentioned in Acts (2:42) includes the teaching received together, the sharing of meals, and common prayer. It is living side by side in the same faith.
4. Finally, communion is expressed through material gifts offered in love. When the churches make a "contribution" for the mother church in Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8:4 and 9:13), this gesture is not just a simple act of help, but a gift that manifests the fraternal unity among believers from different regions.
G2842.origine: The Greek word κοινωνία (koinōnia) comes from the root κοιν- (koin-), which means "common." It is formed from κοινός (koinós), "belonging to several, shared." The basic image is therefore that of something passing from one to another, of mutual participation. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the Greek translators rendered this word with the idea of common possession or association (as in Leviticus 6:2). The Greek word always emphasizes the relational aspect: not just possessing the same thing, but possessing it together and thus being bound by it.
G2842.emploi: The word κοινωνία appears 16 times in the New Testament. It is very present in Paul (Corinthians, Philippians, Galatians, Philemon), in Hebrews, and in the epistles of John. Acts 2:42 gives the most encompassing sense: "fraternal communion" is a distinctive mark of the early Church, alongside teaching, breaking of bread, and prayer. Paul often uses it to speak of the personal relationship with Christ or participation in the mysteries of salvation: we communicate with Christ (1 Corinthians 1:9), with His blood and body (1 Corinthians 10:16), in His sufferings (Philippians 3:10). But the word also designates very concrete fraternal solidarity: the churches of Macedonia and Achaia feel linked to the poor in Jerusalem and manifest their unity through gifts (Romans 15:26; 2 Corinthians 8-9). Thus, the word ranges from the most spiritual to the most material, always uniting the personal bond and the act of love.
G2842.portee: For the believer today as in the past, communion speaks of two inseparable realities: a deep relationship with Christ at the heart of faith, and a lived fraternity with other members of the body of Christ. The word frees us from the illusion of a solitary faith: being a Christian means being admitted into a communion, that is, into a sharing that engages the whole being — spirit, heart, and hands to serve. It is also a call to solidarity: communion does not remain a beautiful spiritual idea; it is proven by the impulse of the heart that drives one to give and support their brothers.

sens: Disposition to share, to freely give what one possesses
Character of one who willingly communicates with others
Openness of heart towards others
G2843.detail:
1. Generosity is the ability and willingness to give, to share one's possessions without calculation or restraint. It is the opposite of greed or selfishness. In 1 Timothy 6:18, Paul encourages to be "rich in good works" and to have generosity: it is about putting one's money at the service of others and the community.
2. This word also evokes a certain natural openness: the ability to communicate easily, to empathize with others, to show kindness in relationships. It is an attitude of heart that translates into concrete actions.
3. Biblical generosity is not a mere occasional gesture, but a habitual disposition, a way of being turned towards the good of others.
G2843.origine: The word comes from the Greek κοινωνία (koinônia), which means "communion," "sharing," "association." It is formed from the verb κοινωνέω (koinôneô), "to share" or "to have in common." The root κοινός (koinós) means "common." The adjective κοινωνικός thus describes one who embodies this logic of sharing and commonality: someone communicative and generous by nature.
G2843.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:18. Paul uses it in a context of exhortation to the rich: he does not ask them to renounce their possessions, but to use them generously, doing good and sharing. Generosity is presented as an essential virtue of one who possesses, a concrete manifestation of faith and love for one's neighbor. It is a disposition that the wealthy Christian must cultivate to avoid succumbing to the trap of wealth.
G2843.portee: For the Christian, this entry reminds that generosity is not a secondary virtue, but a mark of spiritual maturity. Wealthy believers are called to see their possessions not as exclusive ownership, but as a means to serve and support the community. Generosity frees from the corrupting power of money and concretely expresses love for one's neighbor.

sens: Person who shares an activity, task, work with another
Person who has a share in something, who shares a condition or experience
One who has communion with, who participates in the life or practices of a group
G2844.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a person linked to another by a professional or practical association: they work together or for the same cause. James and John are the "partners" of Simon in the fishing trade (Luke 5:10); Titus is Paul's "partner" in his service to the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23). It is a true company of work.
2. A partner is also someone who shares a common experience or condition—often a trial. Christians who remained faithful despite persecutions have "part" in the sufferings (2 Corinthians 1:7); those who associate with the confessors of the faith experience their trials with them (Hebrews 10:33).
3. The word finally designates one who has communion with someone or something, in the sense of participating in the same life or the same rites. Eating a sacrifice at the altar is to be in "communion" with that altar (1 Corinthians 10:18); sharing in the practices of demons is to enter into "communion" with them (1 Corinthians 10:20). It is an intimate participation.
G2844.origine: The word comes from κοινός (common, shared): a partner is literally one who shares the common, who has nothing separate. In Hebrew, it notably translates חָבֵר (friend, companion), derived from a root meaning "to bind together." The family of the Greek word includes κοινωνία (communion, participation, sharing), which is very frequent in the New Testament.
G2844.emploi: The word appears 10 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul. It primarily refers to companions in work or ministry (Luke, 2 Corinthians). In Paul, it particularly acquires a strong spiritual significance: it describes one who shares a trial with other believers, or who enters into communion—meaning real participation—with a spiritual reality (the altar, demons, grace). The meaning shifts from practical partnership to mystical communion, always retaining the idea of sharing in common.
G2844.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Christian faith is not solitary: one is always associated with others, with the apostles, with those who suffer, with the life of Christ himself. To be a "partner" is to share: to share work, trials, consolation, and ultimately the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). It is a call to real communion, not superficial.

sens: furniture where one sleeps
marital bed, marital union
sexual act, illicit or not
G2845.detail:
1. The bed is the furniture where one rests and sleeps. When the importunate friend knocks at the door, the family responds: "my children and I are in bed" (Luke 11:7), meaning they are lying down and cannot get up.
2. The marital bed refers to the bond of marriage, the intimate union between spouses. The letter to the Hebrews calls Christians to honor marriage and to keep the bed "undefiled" (Hebrews 13:4), meaning to respect marital fidelity.
3. By extension, the word can also refer to the sexual act itself, legitimate within marriage or illicit outside of it. Paul lists the vices that Christians must avoid, naming "licentiousness" alongside excesses and quarrels (Romans 13:13), which includes disordered sexual relations.
G2845.origine: The Greek word κοίτη is a feminine noun from the verb κεῖμαι, "to lie down." It literally designates the place where one lies down to rest. The Greek Old Testament primarily uses it to translate the Hebrew word משׁכּב (mishkav), which has the same concrete meaning and the same figurative range (rest, marital relationship, sexual act).
G2845.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, with two main meanings depending on the context. In the literal and material sense, it is the bed where one sleeps (Luke 11:7, Romans 9:10 with the nuanced sense of conception, thus of carnal union). In the figurative or moral sense, it is the marital bed and, by metonymy, the sexual act it represents. In Hebrews 13:4, the context is clearly that of marriage to be honored. In Romans 13:13, on the contrary, the word is included in a list of vices, designating immoral sexual relations outside of marriage.
G2845.portee: This word reminds Christians that marriage and the marital relationship are physical realities that God honors when they remain faithful and pure, but which can become traps of sin if they escape His order. The Bible does not despise the body and the rest of the bed, but situates them under God's gaze, calling for sobriety and chastity.

sens: Officer of the royal household responsible for the king's chamber and private apartments
Trusted servant of the sovereign in charge of domestic affairs
By extension, high official or minister of the king
G2846.detail:
1. The chamberlain is literally the man in charge of the king's bedroom (κοίτη means "bed," "chamber"). He is a high-ranking officer in the royal household, responsible for the sovereign's private apartments and everything related to them. In Acts 12:20, Herod's chamberlain is an important figure since the Tyrians and Sidonians seek him out to gain favor with the king.
2. The chamberlain is above all a trusted servant: to have access to the royal chamber and manage the king's intimate affairs, one must enjoy absolute trust. This closeness to supreme power makes him a key interlocutor, a powerful intermediary between subjects and the monarch.
3. The title can more broadly refer to a minister or high-ranking officer in the service of the king, tasked with official missions beyond mere domestic management. By winning over Herod's chamberlain, the Tyrians and Sidonians hope to influence the king himself.
G2846.origine: The word comes from the Greek κοίτη (koité), which means "bed" or "bedroom" — the quintessential private space. The suffix -ών indicates a charge or function. The Greek word translates the Hebrew חֶדֶר (khéder), which also refers to a chamber or private room, particularly in descriptions of the temple or royal house. This etymology reminds us that the chamberlain derives his prestige from his proximity to the most secret and sacred space of royal power.
G2846.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 12:20, where it refers to the chamberlain of King Herod Agrippa. He is a sufficiently high-ranking officer to be the subject of diplomatic negotiations: the delegates from Tyre and Sidon specifically seek him out and make advances to gain his favor and, through him, that of the king. The usage shows that the chamberlain is a real political figure, a point of contact between the king and those who desire his audience or goodwill. The context also reveals the moral implication: in the story, it is through the intervention of the chamberlain that the king's hostile relations with these cities begin to improve.
G2846.portee: The chamberlain reminds us that real political power often passes through personal relationships and access to high officials, rather than through direct official channels. For the reader, this detail in Acts shows how God governs even the intrigues of the court: the mere fact that a chamberlain is "won over" changes the course of affairs between nations. It is also a lesson on discreet influence and trust: those who have the ear of power shape events.

sens: bright red or purple color obtained by dyeing
fabric or garment of this color
luxury and material wealth
symbol of sin or guilt
G2847.detail: 1. The word describes a bright red color, one of the most beautiful and precious in antiquity. In Hebrews 9:19, Moses uses scarlet wool during the sprinkling of the blood of the covenant — a color chosen for its magnificence and solemn symbolism of purification. 2. By extension, it refers to fabrics or garments dyed this color, a sign of wealth and status. In Revelation 17:4, the woman is clothed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and precious stones: this is the display of earthly luxury and power. 3. Scarlet represents material wealth and the splendor of luxury. In Revelation 18:12 and 18:16, scarlet is listed among the most expensive goods of trade — gold, silk, precious stones — symbolizing earthly and fleeting prosperity. 4. In Matthew 27:28, the scarlet robe thrown on Jesus at the time of the Passion mocks his kingship, but also reflects the guilt and contempt with which men cover him: scarlet here becomes the garment of humiliation and sin.
G2847.origine: The Greek word κόκκινος comes from κόκκος, which refers to the berry or seed. In ancient times, scarlet dye was derived from a parasitic insect found on certain oaks (the ilex coccifera): this intense red was thus "the red of the seed" of this tree. In Hebrew, several biblical terms — תּוֹלָע (tôlâ, the worm) and שָׁנִי (shânî, scarlet) — refer to this same origin: the word literally meant "from the worm" or "from the berry." This natural richness explains why scarlet symbolized luxury, power, and the sacred throughout antiquity.
G2847.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, exclusively in its classical form "scarlet." It first appears in Matthew, who recounts how the Roman soldiers dress Jesus in a scarlet robe in mockery of his supposed kingship. In Hebrews 9:19, the scarlet wool accompanies the solemn rite of the Sinai covenant, marking the importance of the moment. Revelation concentrates the other five occurrences: it uses this word to describe the beast of Revelation (17:3), the woman sitting on it adorned with corrupt luxury (17:4), and finally the luxurious goods of earthly trade destined to perish (18:12, 18:16). The meaning varies according to the context: respect and power at Sinai, mockery and humiliation in Matthew, debauchery and perdition in Revelation.
G2847.portee: This word reminds the believer that luxury and material power, as dazzling as they may seem, are fragile and morally empty. The scarlet robe thrown on Jesus symbolizes how the world cloaks in shame the one whom God honors. For the reader of Revelation, seeing Babylon adorned in scarlet and purple before its destruction is a lesson: earthly beauty deceives, and the appearance of power is but vanity. The scarlet of Sinai, on the other hand, reminds us that it is God alone who gives meaning to color and splendor — not human luxury.

sens: Small seed intended to be sown
Seed so tiny that it symbolizes what is insignificant
What dies and germinates to produce fruit
G2848.detail:
1. A grain is a small seed that is sown in the ground to cultivate it. Jesus speaks of the "mustard seed" (a very small seed) that is sown in a field or garden: it becomes a great tree (Luke 13:19).
2. By its extreme smallness, the grain symbolizes insignificance and weakness. Jesus uses it to show that faith, even tiny "like a mustard seed," is capable of doing the impossible — moving a mountain or uprooting a tree (Matthew 17:20; Luke 17:6).
3. The grain also evokes death and resurrection: the grain of wheat that "falls to the ground" and "dies" produces "much fruit" — an image of the resurrection of Christ and the spiritual fruit that results from it (John 12:24).
G2848.origine: The Greek word κόκκος simply refers to a seed or grain. In Hebrew, we find תּוֹלָע (tôlaa') which can also refer to a larva or worm, but in Greek, the meaning has focused on the seed itself. The word comes from a root that perhaps evokes the sound of grain being crushed or ground. In classical Greek, it is already attested with the meaning of seed grain.
G2848.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Gospels and in 1 Corinthians. It is particularly frequent in Jesus' teachings: six times in the first three Gospels and John. Jesus first uses it in parables of the Kingdom (Matthew 13:31; Mark 4:31; Luke 13:19): a tiny grain becomes great. He then uses it as a symbol of faith (Matthew 17:20; Luke 17:6): even minuscule, it transforms everything. Finally, in John 12:24, the grain becomes a metaphor for his own fruitful death: to die is to bear fruit. Paul mentions it once (1 Corinthians 15:37) when speaking of the resurrection: the resurrected body is sown like a grain and rises transformed.
G2848.portee: This word invites the believer to two discoveries: first, that smallness is not a limitation — a tiny faith can accomplish miracles as long as it is genuine. Secondly, that death is not failure but the seed of fruit: following Jesus means consenting to "die" (to sin, to oneself) to bear much fruit in eternal life. It is a word of freedom and hope.

sens: To cut off, to mutilate
To restrain, to stop, to control
To chastise, to correct through punishment
G2849.detail:
1. The word originally comes from the idea of cutting off or mutilating, like pruning a branch: it is the action of cutting or diminishing. This physical image is rarely used in the New Testament.
2. From there, the meaning of restraining or controlling derives: stopping someone in their tracks, thwarting them. It is to slow down an action, to block a movement.
3. The most common meaning is to chastise or punish — to inflict a penalty on someone for their wrongdoing. In Acts 4:21, the authorities do not know how to punish the apostles because of the crowd. In 2 Peter 2:9, God reserves the unjust to be punished on the day of judgment: punishment is then the act of divine justice that recompenses evil.
G2849.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes the idea of cutting off or trimming (κόλος = mutilated, truncated). This initial physical meaning has gradually shifted towards the abstract idea of limiting, stopping, and then punishing — correcting someone as one corrects an act by diminishing or nullifying it through a penalty. It is a natural progression: from the concrete (to cut) to the figurative (to control, then to chastise).
G2849.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 4:21, it is the Jewish authorities who hesitate to punish the apostles; in 2 Peter 2:9, it is God who reserves the unjust to be punished. In both cases, it involves inflicting a penalty in response to an action deemed wrong. The context in Acts is that of human and social judgment (one cannot punish because of the crowd), while in 2 Peter, divine judgment is in view — a future and irrevocable punishment on the day of judgment.
G2849.portee: This word reminds us that sin does not go without consequence. For the believer, it states that God can deliver those who obey Him from trial, while the unjust face certain punishment. It is a source of comfort (God protects His own) and a warning (judgment is real and just).

sens: Flattering or cajoling words intended to please
The attitude or discourse of a person who seeks to seduce through excessive compliments
G2850.detail:
1. Flattery is a sweet and pleasant word addressed to someone to please them, often exaggerating their qualities or saying what one believes they want to hear. Paul asserts to the Thessalonians that he never used such words to persuade them or for his personal gain (1 Thessalonians 2:5).
2. In a broader sense, it is a general attitude of complacency: seeking to seduce through flattering words rather than speaking sincere truth. It is the weapon of those who lack honesty and hide dishonest intentions, such as greed.
G2850.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb κολακεύω (to flatter), which describes the action of one who seeks to please through complacent words. The Greek family of the word evokes the image of someone who becomes an adulator or servile to gain an advantage. It is a Greek word used to stigmatize a defect of the heart: insincerity.
G2850.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 2:5. Paul uses it to justify himself before the young Christians in Thessalonica: he asserts that he never sought to win them over with flattering compliments or lies. He explicitly contrasts flattery with sincere honesty and the absence of seeking personal profit. It is a word used in a context of apostolic authenticity and relational trust.
G2850.portee: This word reminds Christians that sincerity and honesty are fundamental in our relationships with one another, especially in the ministry of the Word. Flattery, even when well-intentioned, undermines trust and diverts from the truth. It is the enemy of authentic communion in Christ.

sens: Penalty, punishment inflicted for a fault or a shortcoming
Correction, discipline aimed at amending the one who undergoes it
Fear of divine judgment
G2851.detail:
1. Punishment is primarily a concrete penalty inflicted on one who has committed a fault: it is the sanction for disobedience. In Matthew 25:46, Jesus speaks of the "eternal punishment" reserved for those who did not help the little ones — it is the definitive and irreversible consequence of God's judgment.
2. Beyond simple punishment, the word can also refer to disciplinary correction, like that of a teacher correcting a student to train and improve them. This dimension is less emphasized in the New Testament.
3. In 1 John 4:18, "fear involves punishment": it is the fear of judgment that torments one who is not assured of God's love. Here, punishment is not so much the act as the threat, weighing on the conscience.
G2851.origine: The word comes from the verb κολάζω (to strike, to correct). Originally, it denotes correction or discipline, but it comes to mean primarily a penalty or punishment. The Greek word translates in the Old Testament the Hebrew כָּלַם (to cover with shame) and other terms related to correction or penalty. The biblical notion of punishment is always linked to God's justice: it is never arbitrary, but a response to disobedience.
G2851.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Matthew 25:46, it refers to eternal punishment, destined for the cursed on the day of judgment — it is a definitive act of God. In 1 John 4:18, it takes on a psychological hue: the "fear of punishment" is what paralyzes one whose relationship with God is not based on love, but on fear of condemnation. Both uses emphasize God's future judgment.
G2851.portee: For the believer, this word invites us to take seriously the reality of divine judgment, but also to understand that the perfect love of the Father in Jesus Christ frees us from fear. It reminds us that disobedience has eternal consequences, while showing that one who remains in God's love does not fear this punishment.

sens: To hit someone with a closed fist or the back of the hand
To slap, to hit roughly
To mistreat, to beat
To humiliate or torment morally
G2852.detail:
1. The basic meaning is literally to strike with the fist or the back of the hand. This is what happens to Jesus during his trial: the guards "struck him with fists and slapped him" (Matthew 26:67), or struck him "with blows" (Mark 14:65).
2. The word can also refer to a more humiliating blow, such as a slap or a slap to the face. It is an act of contempt and insult, not just brute force.
3. In a broader sense, it means to mistreat someone, to hit repeatedly. Paul says of the apostles that they are "mistreated" (1 Corinthians 4:11), which evokes a series of violent trials.
4. The word can also express moral or spiritual torment: Paul speaks of "a messenger of Satan to buffet me," an image of punishment or a thorn that prevents pride (2 Corinthians 12:7). It is to strike in the sense of afflicting the soul.
G2852.origine: The Greek word comes from the name κόλαφος, which refers to a closed fist or the joints of the fingers. The starting image is therefore that of the fist striking. The verb is formed to mean "to strike with the fist." In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates Hebrew words that describe blows or physical violence.
G2852.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, mainly to describe violence against people. Three uses are in the literal and historical sense: the blows inflicted on Jesus during his interrogation (Matthew and Mark), acts of mockery and torture. Paul uses it twice to speak of the sufferings of the apostles: once for common physical mistreatment (1 Corinthians 4:11), and once for a spiritual or moral torment described as a thorn that "buffets" him (2 Corinthians 12:7). Peter uses it to encourage Christians to endure mistreatment with dignity (1 Peter 2:20). The word always carries a nuance of insult or contempt, never a simple correction.
G2852.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of the physical and moral suffering that Jesus and the apostles endured for the Gospel. It shows that the disciple is not above his master: if Jesus suffered blows and humiliations, the Christian should not expect to be spared. At the same time, the word invites dignity: Peter encourages believers to endure these trials without compromising their faith, for it is a "grace in the sight of God." It is a call to perseverance in adversity.

sens: To stick, to firmly attach two material things together
To adhere to someone, to follow them, to stand by their side
To choose someone or something strongly, to hold on firmly
To unite with someone, particularly in the sense of marriage or physical intimacy
To draw closer to someone or something, becoming near to it
G2853.detail:
1. The verb first describes the physical action of sticking, of fixing together: it is the image of glue that unites two surfaces. In Luke 10:11, dust clings to the feet of the disciples — it adheres physically to them.
2. It is then the act of joining a group, of becoming a companion to someone: in Acts 9:26, Saul seeks to join the apostles, to become one with them; in Acts 5:13, others dared not join the apostles, meaning to become their companions.
3. It is a firm and lasting choice: in Acts 17:34, some clung to Paul and believed, suggesting a deep and stable adherence. In Romans 12:9, one clings to what is good, choosing it as an inseparable companion.
4. The word describes the intimate union of marriage: in Matthew 19:5, a man clings to his wife, expressing the deepest marital bond. This attachment is both physical and spiritual.
5. Finally, it is to draw physically closer: in Acts 8:29, the Spirit tells Philip to approach the chariot of the Ethiopian minister — to come close enough to speak to him.
G2853.origine: The word comes from κόλλα (kolla), glue. It is the image of a sticky substance that firmly unites two elements. In Hebrew, this verb mainly translates דָּבַק (davaq), which carries exactly the same physical image: to adhere, to stick, to cling. Like glue, the attachment described here is something solid and lasting — a union that cannot be separated without effort.
G2853.emploi: The verb κολλάω appears about twelve times in the New Testament. It is used in the passive (with a form like "to cling to") to describe the action of someone who joins someone or something. In Acts, it recounts how disciples or others join people or groups: Saul wants to join the apostles, some cling to Paul. In Romans and 1 Corinthians, Paul uses it more figuratively: to cling to what is good, to the Lord, or the physical union in marriage. The meaning varies slightly depending on the context — physical here, moral or spiritual there — but the idea of fixation, of close adherence remains constant.
G2853.portee: Understanding this verb helps the reader grasp the strength of the personal attachment that the Bible encourages. When Paul says "cling to the Lord" or "to what is good," it is not a vague feeling: it is a union as solid as that of glue, a decision that binds us. Similarly, marriage in Matthew 19:5 is not a light contract, but a deep adherence of the whole person. This word invites us to examine what or whom we truly cling to — our choices and our bonds reveal our spiritual priorities.

sens: Medical ointment in the form of a small cake or tablet, applied to the eyes for healing
Figuratively, that which heals spiritual blindness and restores vision
G2854.detail:
1. The word literally refers to an ointment for the eyes, in the form of a small cake or solid tablet. It is a remedy applied directly to the eyes to treat vision ailments. In Revelation 3:18, Christ offers it to the disciples of Laodicea so that they may see: it is the concrete treatment for a common physical infirmity.

2. The eye salve also represents spiritually the remedy for the blindness of the soul — the inability to recognize the truth of God. When Christ tells the Laodiceans "so that you may see," he speaks of regaining spiritual sight, of finally perceiving the reality of their condition and the help he offers. The visible remedy becomes the image of inner healing.
G2854.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek κόλλιξ (kollix), which referred to a coarse cake in the shape of a round cake or tablet. The diminutive suffix -ούριον makes it smaller and more precise: it is a tablet or small round cake. By extension, the word designated an eye remedy shaped in the same way — a solid tablet that could be rubbed on the eyelids. It is a very specialized word, limited to medical vocabulary and the text of Revelation.
G2854.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 3:18. Christ offers it to the Christians of Laodicea, a wealthy but spiritually blind city. Revelation contrasts the material prosperity of the Laodiceans with their spiritual poverty: they think they are rich and fulfilled, but they do not see their misery. The eye salve that Christ offers them is the only remedy for this blindness. This image draws from the medical reality of the 1st century — eye salves were known and common pharmaceutical products — to express a radical transformation of spiritual vision.
G2854.portee: This word reminds us that spiritual blindness is a real disease that deprives us of seeing God and his truth. But it also affirms that this blindness is not incurable: Christ offers the remedy. The image of the eye salve suggests that healing requires accepting what we do not initially see, receiving Christ's treatment as one would receive a medication. It is a call to recognize that we have lost our vision and to plead with the One who can restore it.

sens: Merchant who exchanges currencies
One who converts foreign coins into temple coins
Vendor set up in the temple to facilitate pilgrims' transactions
G2855.detail:
1. A money changer is a merchant specialized in currency exchange. At the temple in Jerusalem, pilgrims arriving from distant regions needed to convert their foreign coins into local currency, accepted for offerings and ritual purchases.

2. The money changer operated in the temple courtyard, where he bought foreign coins and sold the appropriate Jewish coins, taking a commission in the process. John 2:15 mentions that Jesus "drove out the money changers," highlighting the importance and quantity of coins handled in these exchanges.

3. These money changers worked alongside the sellers of pigeons (animals necessary for sacrifices). Matthew and Mark place them together in the temple, forming a commercial system that had developed to serve the pilgrims, but which Jesus perceives as a desecration of the holy place.
G2855.origine: The Greek word κολλυβιστής comes from κόλλυβος, which refers to a small coin or an exchange rate. This root evokes the concrete image of small coins handled during transactions. The word thus arises from the commercial reality: one who deals with small coins becomes "the specialist of small coins" or more broadly, one who deals with exchange rates.
G2855.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the account of Jesus cleansing the temple: Matthew 21:12, Mark 11:15, and John 2:15. In these three parallel or closely related passages, it refers to the same merchants operating in the sacred precinct. The absence of the word outside this context shows that the evangelist uses it to precisely describe this commercial activity of the temple, without exploring other dimensions or uses.
G2855.portee: These three passages reveal Jesus' prophetic anger at the commercialization of the place of worship. The cleansing of the temple is not merely a matter of cleanliness, but an act of messianic authority: Jesus challenges an established system that had turned the house of prayer into a "den of thieves." For the modern believer, this word reminds us that authentic piety cannot be hindered or exploited by commercial interests, even if legalized or practical; it is a call to sincerity in worship.

sens: To cut, remove a part of something
To reduce the duration of a period
To limit, reduce the extent or intensity of something
G2856.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to cut or remove a part of an object (hence the image of the Greek word, which evokes something that is shortened or truncated). This is the meaning retained in the Greek Old Testament when speaking of things that are cut or amputated.

2. In the Gospels, this physical meaning expands to duration: to shorten days means to reduce their number or length. In Matthew 24:22 and Mark 13:20, Jesus speaks of "shortened" days — it is not about mechanically shortening each day, but limiting the total number of days of tribulation, so that the elect are not annihilated.

3. More broadly, the verb evokes the idea of restricting, circumscribing: reducing something to its essentials, limiting its scope or effect. This is why it can apply not only to time but to any reality one wishes to contain or diminish.
G2856.origine: The Greek word comes from the adjective « kolóbos » (shortened, truncated), which expresses the idea of something that is amputated or mutilated. The root refers to an action of cutting or separating. In Hebrew, the verb « qatzatz » (קָצַץ) in the sense of "to cut" or "to remove" expresses a similar notion. This lexical field of separation and limitation is common in ancient languages to speak of both physical actions and more abstract realities like time.
G2856.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, solely in the two synoptic Gospels of Matthew and Mark, in an identical apocalyptic context. Jesus uses it to describe divine intervention at the end of times: God will shorten the days of tribulation, not inadvertently, but deliberately "for the sake of the elect." The verb emphasizes here the sovereign and merciful action of God: rather than allowing evil to spread indefinitely and annihilate His elect, the Lord intervenes to limit the duration of the trial. The use of the verb, although rare, is therefore loaded with theological meaning.
G2856.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that God is not passive in the face of His people's suffering. In times of trial and tribulation, the Lord exercises His sovereignty not to prolong distress, but to limit it and protect His own. It is a word of hope: dark days have an end, set by divine mercy. This truth strengthens faith amid difficulties.

sens: City of Phrygia in ancient Asia Minor, located in the valley of the Lycus
G2857G.detail: Colossae is a city in the region of Phrygia, in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), situated in the valley of the Lycus River. It is a city of secondary importance in the geography of the Greco-Roman world, but it becomes famous in Christian history because Paul founds a church there and addresses an epistle to it (Colossians 1:2).
G2857G.origine: The Greek name Kolossai simply designates this ancient city. The region of Phrygia was known for its commerce and trade, and Colossae was located on important trade routes connecting the major cities of Roman Asia Minor. The name itself has a local origin, the precise meaning of which eludes us.
G2857G.emploi: Colossae is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 1:2, where Paul greets the church of this city. This unique mention speaks volumes about the importance Paul attaches to this community: although Colossae is not a metropolis like Ephesus or Antioch, Paul takes care to address an entire letter to its members. The epistle to the Colossians reveals that this church is facing false teachings, and Paul provides his apostolic corrections.

sens: Inhabitant of Colossae, a city of Phrygia in Asia Minor
G2858.detail: 1. Inhabitant of Colossae, an important city in the Roman province of Asia (in modern-day Turkey). Paul addresses his epistle to the Colossians, meaning the Christians of this city who received the Gospel. The word simply designates geographical origin and belonging to this ecclesial community.
G2858.origine: Κολασσαεύς comes from the name of the city Κολοσσαί (Colossae). Colossae was a prosperous city in Phrygia, in the valley of the Lycus, alongside Laodicea and Hierapolis. Its Greek name is formed with the suffix -εύς, which designates the inhabitant or native of a place.
G2858.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, at the end of the epistle to the Colossians (Colossians 4:18), where Paul greets the Colossian brothers. Although the technical term is rarely used, the entire epistle is addressed to this community. Colossae did not receive a direct visit from Paul, but Epaphras brought the Christian faith there. The epistle deals with false doctrines threatening this church and reaffirms the absolute supremacy of Christ.
G2858.portee: Understanding that Paul addresses real believers in a real city allows us to see the epistle to the Colossians not as an abstract doctrine, but as a concrete pastoral letter, intended for a community facing specific spiritual challenges. This reminds us that the Gospel takes root everywhere in the real world, from the Levant to the heart of Roman Asia Minor.

sens: The lap or chest of a person
The pocket formed by the folds of a garment
A bay or a gulf
Intimacy and emotional closeness
Heaven or divine favor
G2859.detail:
1. The breast primarily refers to the lap or chest of a person — the place where someone holds a child close, or where one rests in intimacy. This is how the disciple "was reclining on the breast of Jesus" (John 13:23), a posture of affection and absolute trust. Similarly, the Son is said to be "in the bosom of the Father" (John 1:18), an image of eternity and divine unity.

2. The breast can also refer to the folds of a garment that hang over the waist and form a sort of pocket: this is where small objects were carried or where one would gather what was generously poured out. Jesus says that if one gives, "it will be poured into your bosom in good measure" (Luke 6:38), evoking this image of a garment overflowing with what is placed in it.

3. The breast can also refer to a bay or a natural hollow, as in "a bay" where Paul and his companions could have run aground the ship (Acts 27:39).

4. Spiritually, the "bosom of Abraham" expresses intimacy with the patriarch and, by extension, rest and communion with the people of God in heaven. Lazarus rests there (Luke 16:22-23), a sign of eternal comfort after his earthly suffering.
G2859.origine: The Greek word kolpos comes from a root describing something that is hollow or folded. It translates the Hebrew héiq, which has the same concrete meaning of "lap" or "breast." The metaphor of the breast as a place of intimacy, rest, or closeness is common to both testaments: it evokes a relationship of love and trust, as well as protection.
G2859.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Segond, concentrated in the Gospels of Luke and John. Luke primarily uses it in the sense of pocket (the garment that generously receives in Luke 6:38) and to describe eternal rest in the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16:22-23). John uses it to express emotional intimacy with Jesus (13:23) and the eternal relationship of the Son to the Father (1:18). There is a single occurrence in Acts (27:39) that refers to a maritime bay. The word thus transitions from the concrete sense (the physical lap) to the figurative sense (spiritual intimacy, divine protection).
G2859.portee: This word speaks to us of closeness to God and total trust. To rest on someone's breast means to accept their love unreservedly: this is what the beloved disciple does with Jesus, and it is our place when we surrender to divine grace. The promise of the bosom of Abraham also reminds us that our sufferings are not final: we await eternal communion with God. Finally, giving generously "into the bosom" means that our giving to others rebounds as divine blessing in our lives.

sens: To move in water by making body movements
To jump into the water to cross or escape
G2860.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of moving in water by coordinated body movements — this is swimming in the literal sense, as one would do today at the sea or in a river. In Acts 27:43, during the shipwreck of the vessel carrying Paul to Rome, the centurion "ordered those who could swim to jump in the water first to reach the land": this is a life-saving swim, where the sailors must reach the shore.
2. Practically, the word can also evoke the action of diving or jumping into the water voluntarily to cover a distance or escape danger — the image of someone resolutely entering the water to save themselves or to progress.
G2860.origine: The word comes from a root that describes movement in water. The verb was known in classical Greek to denote the action of swimming or diving. It appears only once in the New Testament, but the Greeks of the time, a seafaring people, were well acquainted with this gesture.
G2860.emploi: The verb κολυμβάω appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:43. It is during the account of the shipwreck in the Mediterranean: the ship is broken, and the soldiers and sailors must jump into the water to reach the shore. The centurion has the best swimmers go first to ensure safety and find a way to land. The context is one of life-threatening urgency, where knowing how to swim is a practical survival skill.
G2860.portee: For the reader, this verb reminds us of the concrete humanity of the apostle Paul: he is not spared from the ordinary dangers of ancient navigation. The shipwreck in Acts 27 shows that faith in God coexists with the realities of the body and the skills necessary for survival. It also provides a window into Mediterranean life and the perils that preachers faced in bringing the Gospel.

sens: A basin filled with water where one can swim or bathe
A reservoir of water used for washing and purification
G2861.detail: 1. A pool is a basin of water, generally large enough for swimming or immersion. This is how the pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem is designated, a public place with five porticoes where the sick gathered, waiting for the water to be stirred to receive healing (John 5:2, 4). 2. The word also refers to a reservoir of water used for washing and purification. This is the case with the pool of Siloam, where Jesus sends the blind man to wash after anointing his eyes (John 9:7). Although one can technically swim there, the emphasis here is on water as a means of purification and restoration.
G2861.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "to swim" (kolumbáô) and thus designates a place where one swims. It translates the Hebrew "bérékah" (בְּרֵכָה), which means "basin" or "pond." The word evokes the practical image of a space of water deep and spacious enough for immersion or free movement.
G2861.emploi: The word appears only five times in the New Testament, exclusively in John. It is first used for the pool of Bethesda (John 5:2, 4, 7), a place of healing where the sick and infirm converge in expectation of a miracle. John highlights the central role of this pool in the Israelites' hope for salvation before the coming of Jesus. Then, the same word designates the pool of Siloam (John 9:7, 9:11), where the blind man washes and regains his sight. In both cases, the water basin is the setting for a divine intervention: miraculous healing or restoration of sight. The biblical context shows that the pool is less a mere bathing place than a space where water plays a role of transformation and salvation.
G2861.portee: These two miracle accounts at the pool teach the reader that Jesus is the true healer and the one who brings salvation, beyond earthly hopes placed in water or remedies. At Bethesda, crowds await an endless miracle; at Siloam, Jesus acts personally and changes lives. The pool thus becomes a symbol of all insufficient human resources and the universal need for transformation that only Jesus can provide.

sens: establishment founded by Rome in conquered territory, inhabited by Roman citizens
city endowed with the status and rights of a Roman city
G2862.detail:
1. A Roman colony is a city created by Rome in a conquered region, where Roman citizens live while retaining their rights and status. It enjoys local autonomy while remaining linked to the Roman state. Philippi, in Macedonia, had this status of a colony (Acts 16:12): it was a city of Roman citizens established in Greek territory.
2. By extension, a colony is simply a city established according to this Roman model, with its own institutions and rights, which distinguished it from other cities in the territory. This status confers particular prestige and privileges to its inhabitants.
G2862.origine: The word κολωνία comes directly from the Latin "colonia," borrowed by Greek because this administrative system was specific to Rome. "Colonia" originally refers to an agricultural or military settlement founded by Roman settlers. The French word "colonie" is derived from it. The concept itself has no direct equivalent in Hebrew from the Old Testament: it is a purely Roman reality of the New Testament.
G2862.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 16:12, when Paul and Silas arrive in Philippi in Macedonia. Luke explicitly mentions that Philippi is "the leading city of a district of Macedonia, and a colony." This historical precision emphasizes that Philippi was not an ordinary Greek city, but a Roman city established in Macedonian territory, with its Roman institutions and Roman citizens. This detail makes the subsequent events intelligible: the authority of the magistrates (Acts 16:20-22) and the rights of Roman citizens.
G2862.portee: The word "colony" reminds us that at the time of Paul, Rome dominated the Mediterranean world and imposed its political order. For the reader, it is a subtle indication that the Gospel penetrates to the centers of Roman power, in the cities where the citizens of the empire live. It also highlights how Paul's presence in these places exposed the nascent Church to the structures of Roman domination, from which it was ultimately independent.

sens: to have long hair
to let one's hair grow
G2863.detail:
1. To wear long hair: this means having hair that extends in length, as opposed to a shaved head or short hair. The Apostle Paul mentions this practice in 1 Corinthians 11:14, where he refers to it as something that can be a "shame" for a man in the culture of his time.
2. To let one's hair grow: the verb describes the action of not cutting one's hair, allowing it to grow naturally. It is a visible gesture that distinguishes the one who does it from others; this is why it can have significant cultural or religious meaning in a given community.
G2863.origine: The Greek word comes from κόμη (komê), which literally means "hair" or "hairstyle." The verb κομάω (komaō) is simply formed from the noun by adding the verbal ending -άω, transforming the object (having hair) into action (wearing hair, cultivating it). This formation is direct and concrete: the verb describes the state of one who possesses long hair.
G2863.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in 1 Corinthians 11:14-15, in the passage where Paul addresses the issue of hair length in relation to the distinctions between men and women in the assembly. In 1 Corinthians 11:14, Paul asks: "Does not nature itself teach you that it is a shame for a man to have long hair?" In 1 Corinthians 11:15, he concludes: "But if a woman has long hair, it is her glory" (where the same verb appears or is closely related). The context shows that Paul uses this vocabulary to address cultural conventions and ecclesiastical practices of his time.
G2863.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not ignore concrete cultural realities — clothing, appearance, hair — and that it can guide Christians on these subjects. However, Paul does not establish an eternal law, but calls for honoring certain cultural conventions out of respect and clarity in the assembly. This invites the reader to distinguish between permanent spiritual principles and cultural applications that vary according to places and times.

sens: The entirety of the hair that covers the head
The hair as a natural adornment or ornament of the body
What covers or veils the body, as a garment would
G2864.detail:
1. The word refers to the entirety of the hair that grows on the head and covers it — it is the complete hairstyle, not an isolated hair. In 1 Corinthians 11:15, Paul speaks of a woman's hair as a physical and visible reality.
2. The hair is presented as a natural adornment, a beauty that a woman possesses by her very creation. It is thus an ornament of the body, comparable to clothing or an accessory.
3. Paul uses the image of hair as a veil — something that naturally covers. When he says that "her hair was given to her as a veil," he means that long hair serves to cover and preserve a woman's dignity, much like a piece of fabric would.
G2864.origine: The Greek word κόμη (komē) refers to hair as the entirety that crowns the head. In ancient Hebrew, words like פֶּרַע (péroa') also refer to hair. The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of what grows, what flourishes — hair as a natural growth of the body.
G2864.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 11:15. Paul addresses the issue of women wearing long hair in the context of worship and prayer. He asserts that it is a "glory" for a woman to wear hair, as it has been given to her naturally as a veil. This statement fits into his argument about the difference in roles and dignity between men and women in the Church. Hair thus becomes a symbol of honorable distinction and natural protection.
G2864.portee: This verse reminds us that the human body, in its created form, carries a wisdom and beauty that God has inscribed in it. For Paul, a woman's hair is not a trivial detail, but a sign of dignity and protection. This invites the Christian to view their body not as something shameful, but as bearing a glory that comes from God — and therefore to treat it with respect in the context of church life.

sens: To take or bring something in a concrete manner
To obtain in return what is due or promised
To receive a reward or punishment according to one's deeds
To finally obtain what one has long awaited
G2865.detail:
1. In its simplest and most concrete sense, the verb means to bring, transport, or deliver something: the sinful woman "brought" an alabaster jar of perfume to Jesus' feet (Luke 7:37). It conveys the idea of taking something in hand and bringing it back.

2. To receive in return or recover what belongs to you: the servant should return the money to the master who, upon his return, would have "taken back" the capital with interest (Matthew 25:27). It is to obtain again what was entrusted to you.

3. To receive what one deserves, for good or for ill, according to one's actions — a divine recompense that corresponds to conduct: each will "receive" according to the good or evil he has done (2 Corinthians 5:10), or according to his injustice (Colossians 3:25). It is to be treated justly by God based on one's life.

4. To finally obtain, after effort, what has been promised or what one is striving for: believers "obtain" the promise (Hebrews 10:36) or rise to receive what is due to them (Hebrews 11:19). It is to reach the fulfillment of what one hoped for.
G2865.origine: The Greek verb komizô comes from a root that evokes the idea of transporting, carrying, and bringing back safely. The middle form (reflexive form in Greek) — "to carry for oneself" — has come to mean receiving what belongs to someone. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew nasa ("to carry, to lift"), which shows the evolution from concrete meaning to figurative meaning.
G2865.emploi: Komizô appears ten times in the New Testament, particularly in the Pauline epistles and the Epistle to the Hebrews. It first describes concrete acts: bringing an object (Luke 7:37). But its use becomes very theological: it denotes divine recompense at the final judgment (2 Corinthians 5:10, Ephesians 6:8, Colossians 3:25), where each receives according to his works. It also expresses the fulfillment of long-awaited promises (Hebrews 10:36, 11:19, 11:39), notably resurrection and heavenly reward. The Epistle of 1 Peter uses it for receiving the crown of glory (5:4) and the salvation of the soul (1:9). This word thus emphasizes the certainty that God, being just, gives to each according to his work.
G2865.portee: This verb reminds the believer of an essential truth: God never looks at our actions without consequence. Every gesture, every work done for Him and according to His will will lead to true recompense. It is both an exhortation to perseverance and an assurance: even the faithful servant, even the obedient slave, will receive his share of reward from the Lord. The word also calls for moral vigilance: one receives according to what one has sown.

sens: To be in a better state, in better health
To feel better
To progress, to improve
G2866.detail:
1. The word describes the state of a person who is better after an illness or affliction. In John 4:52, the father of the sick boy asks his servants "at what hour" the child became better — he seeks the precise moment when the fever disappeared and the boy regained health. The image is one of physical improvement, tangible and observable.
2. More broadly, "to get better" means to emerge from a state of weakness, suffering, or danger. It is to feel better, to be in better condition. The word evokes a contrast: before, one was unwell; now, one is better.
3. The word can also express a progression or general improvement in a person's circumstances or condition, beyond just physical health.
G2866.origine: The Greek word kompsóteron comes from a root (komé-) that means "to care for, to take care of." It is related to the idea of taking care of oneself, presenting oneself well, or being well. It is a comparative of the word kompsós, which means "elegant, well-arranged, neat." The basic image is that of care given to one's appearance or state; hence it transitions to "to be well," "to feel better." The word has a somewhat familiar or conversational flavor in the Greek of the time.
G2866.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 4:52. It is a pivotal moment in the narrative: Jesus healed the son of a royal official from a distance, simply by His word. The father, who was on his way to join his child, meets his servants and asks them at what hour the child became better. Their response — "Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him" — confirms that the healing occurred at the exact moment Jesus spoke His word. The word "better" here marks the moment of transition from illness to health, and emphasizes that the healing was instantaneous and complete.
G2866.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on what it truly means to be "healed" or "to get better" following an encounter with Jesus. The father's question — "at what hour?" — shows that he seeks to verify that Jesus' word truly had its effect. For the believer, "to get better" is not just a return to a previous state, but a sign of Jesus' power and His ability to instantly transform circumstances. It is an invitation to recognize the signs of grace in the details of our lives.

sens: To coat with whitewash or plaster
To mask the corrupt interior with a beautiful exterior appearance
To present oneself as righteous or pure while hiding hypocrisy
G2867.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the action of coating a surface with whitewash or plaster, to protect or decorate it. This is how tombs were whitened in Israel, making them visible and beautiful to look at (Matthew 23:27).
2. Whitening creates an illusion: what is covered in white appears clean and worthy of respect, while what it hides is dirty or dead. Jesus uses it to describe the hypocrisy of the Pharisees: they appear righteous on the outside, but inside they are full of impurities and malice.
3. Figuratively, to "whiten" someone or something is to falsely justify it, to present it as acceptable when it is guilty or corrupt. Paul thus denounces the high priest who judges him unjustly: it is a "whited wall," an authority that pretends to be just while violating the law (Acts 23:3).
G2867.origine: The Greek word comes from konía, meaning "lime" or "white dust." It is a simple and descriptive verb: it paints the concrete image of whitewash. In Hebrew, the same action is expressed by the verb שִׂיד (sîd), which is found in ancient Israelite texts to speak of whitening stones (Deuteronomy 27:2-4).
G2867.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, always in a critical or ironic sense. In Matthew 23:27, Jesus uses it to criticize hypocrisy: the whitened tombs appear beautiful, but contain death. In Acts 23:3, Paul uses the image sharply to designate an authority that violates justice while pretending to uphold it. The meaning rises each time from the concrete to the moral: the material action of whitening becomes a metaphor for dissimulation and falsehood.
G2867.portee: This word invites the reader to look beyond appearances. For Jesus and His apostles, the outward appearance of respectability can hide deep corruption. It warns us: true justice and true holiness do not consist in appearing good, but in being genuinely so, being honest and pure in heart as well as in action.

sens: Fine particles of dry matter that rise and float in the air
Gesture of rejection or symbolic break
G2868.detail:
1. Dust is literally the fine particles that rise from the ground and form a cloud when disturbed. It is a tangible, concrete image — we see the dust fly when we shake our clothes or walk on a dusty road. In Acts 22:23, the crowd "threw dust in the air," a violent gesture of anger and protest.
2. Shaking the dust off one's feet is a symbolic gesture of break and rejection: it tells those who refuse the Gospel that one will not be among them, that all ties are severed. In Matthew 10:14 and Luke 9:5, Jesus instructs his disciples to shake the dust off the towns that do not receive them — it is a silent but clear testimony: "You have rejected the message of the Kingdom."
